speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last my parliamentary assistant read to the house the text of a press statement regarding the outcome of the prolonged negotiations for a renewal of the international wheat agreement. I now intend to supplement that statement by a brief account of the negotiations and to state the Canadian position with respect to the renewal of the wheat agreement.
The negotiations for a renewal of the agreement began in London in the spring of
1952.	The United States at the outset proposed a price range of $1.90 minimum and $2.50 maximum for a period of four years. Canada saw no hope of an agreement at that level of prices and made an opening proposal of $1.75 minimum and $2.25 maximum, excluding carrying charges, which under the present agreement have amounted to the additional six cents per bushel. Australia indicated general agreement with Canada.
The importers did not make price proposals in London, but indicated that they considered the maximum price of $1.80 in the present agreement to be a fair basis for renewal if that maximum included carrying charges.
In Washington the negotiations began on January 30, 1953, where they had left off in London. The United States, supported by France, repeated its proposal on prices but for a period shorter than four years. Canada and Australia repeated their offer of $1.75 minimum, $2.25 maximum, for a period of four years. At this stage the importers made no proposals whatever.
In order to advance the negotiations the exporters unanimously declared that they would not enter into a new agreement at present maximum or minimum prices. The importers replied that they could contemplate an agreement at prices higher than in the present agreement but that they were not prepared to make a definite proposal unless the exporters were prepared to contemplate an agreement with a maximum below $2.25. The exporters unanimously met this condition by agreeing that a maximum below $2.25 would be acceptable.
The importing countries, then, on February 16, 1953, put forward their first offer of a minimum of $1.40 and a maximum of $1.95, inclusive of carrying charges. At that point there was a good deal of informal probing of the price positions on both sides extending over a period of some days. On March 6, the United States said that it was prepared to accept a maximum price of $2.15, inclusive of carrying charges. Canada and Australia supported the $2.15 maximum price as offering a reasonable basis on which to conclude an agreement for a three-year period with a minimum 50 cents below the maximum. A few days later the importing countries unanimously rejected the $2.15 maximum as unacceptable but indicated that there was some basis for compromise between the views of the exporters and importers.
On March 17, Canada, supported by Australia, declared that although they considered the maximum of $2.15 to be reasonable they were prepared to accept a maximum of $2.10 and a minimum of $1.60 in an effort to bring the views of the exporters and the importers into harmony.
A week later the importers replied to the Canadian and Australian proposals. They unanimously rejected the $2.10 maximum. A substantial number of them, representing well over a majority by number and a high proportion by quantity of wheat purchased under the agreement, declared that they could accept a maximum of $2.05, inclusive of carrying charges and a minimum of $1.55. A smaller number, but representing a substantial quantity of wheat, said that they could not agree to this level. Included was the United Kingdom which adhered to the importers' original offer of minimum $1.40, maximum $1.95.
This marked the turning point of the negotiations on price. The United States and the United Kingdom, being the largest exporter and the largest importer, respectively, held discussions in an effort to bridge the considerable gap that still separated them. Finally, on Thursday last, the United States announced that it was willing to accept the proposal of $1.55 minimum, $2.05 maximum, made by a substantial number of the importers. The United States delegate added that while the administration would, of course, recommend approval by the Senate

Wheat
the maximum price to which he was agreeing carried the possibility of failure of Senate ratification. Australia and Canada fell into line. The United Kingdom, however, said that it was unable to accept a maximum price above $2.00.
When the motion to fix the minimum at $1.55 and the maximum at $2.05 for a period of three years was put before the council, only the United Kingdom voted against it, although a few other importing countries abstained.
I have summarized the course of these prolonged negotiations on prices so that hon. members will realize that there was a good deal of give and take on both sides at this wheat conference. Some people may think that the importing countries scored a victory by bringing the exporters down so far from their original ideas. Other people may think that the exporters did well to bring about an improvement from the levels of the present agreement. I suggest that if there was a victory, it was a victory for common sense. That such a wide measure of agreement was reached is evidence that with patience and perseverance and a generous portion of good will, views which may at one time seem so irreconcilable may be reconciled.
It is unfortunate that the council could not reach a unanimous conclusion. Yet I am impressed not by failure to reach complete unanimity, but rather by the fact that the proposal for a $1.55 to $2.05 range of prices received such a wide measure of support and so little opposition. After all, even the United Kingdom did not disagree with the minimum price of $1.55 and was within 5 cents of agreement at the maximum price.
A good deal more attention seems to be directed to the maximum than to the minimum price. Indeed, I have seen suggestions that the maximum of $2.05 will determine the price at which wheat will be bought and sold under the agreement during the next three years. This, of course, is not necessarily so. The forces of demand and supply are bound to affect the price, regardless of whether or not there is an agreement. The wheat agreement merely fixes the range within which prices can fluctuate.
The maximum price is intended to be a protection to the importing countries against prices for the quantities of wheat in the agreement going above that level, just as the minimum price is intended to protect the exporting countries against prices for the agreement quantities going below that level.
At the maximum the importing countries have rights, not obligations. They can demand that wheat be delivered to them at

that level. But they do not have to take it. If they can buy wheat at cheaper prices they are free to do so, down to the minimum.
In effect, agreement to a maximum is what the exporting countries have to accept to get the importing countries to undertake to buy wheat at the minimum. As far as Canada is concerned, we look upon the minimum as being fully as important as the maximum. It is only because of the minimum that we are prepared to join in the agreement.
The Canadian delegation had, of course, worked for a unanimous recommendation and the government regrets that this was not possible. But it will be agreed, I think, that prices which were opposed by only one country out of 46, and which were approved by all except a very few countries which abstained when the vote was taken, do on the face of it provide a fair and reasonable basis for a renewal of the agreement. And, of course, the difference of 5 cents at the maximum between the United Kingdom and rest of the world is very small indeed and well within the margin of error of any forecast of price trends.
Having been in many negotiations with our good friends from the United Kingdom, I know that they are shrewd and hard bargainers and I respect them for it. Their final effort to bring the maximum price down by 5 cents was quite understandable. In a similar position the Canadian government might have done likewise. We tried very hard indeed to get an agreement at maximum and minimum prices 5 cents better than were finally recommended. It should be clear now, however, after fifteen weeks of negotiation, that an international agreement is possible on the basis of the prices recommended by the council and on no other basis. There is a bare minimum of time left for signature and ratification before the beginning of the new crop year.
The agreement will be open for signature for a period of two weeks. The Canadian delegate has already been authorized to sign on behalf of Canada, and will do so today.
We hope the United Kingdom will also sign. While it is possible, and may be necessary, to have an international wheat agreement without the United Kingdom, that is obviously most undesirable. Canada would not be happy. We would not like to be dealing with our best wheat customer on one basis and with our other customers on another. And the government would regret to see relations between our two countries adversely affected either by failure of the agreement to go ahead because the United

Kingdom did not adhere, or because there was an agreement without the United Kingdom.
During the conference, as my summary has indicated, Canada's chief purpose was to harmonize the views of the importers and the other exporters, in particular the United States. To be perfectly frank, we encouraged the United States to modify their original ideas to the point which we thought would provide a reasonable basis for settlement. From time to time, we led the way. Finally, however, it was clear that any further reductions would jeopardize the chance of acceptance by the United States Senate and would probably be unacceptable to the farmers of Canada and Australia. At that point, fortunately, the main body of the importing countries could agree, and thus the council was in a position to make a recommendation supported by an overwhelming maj ority.
I am confident that the United Kingdom shares our belief in the underlying purposes of the wheat agreement. Their declarations on this point and their agreement with the recommended minimum price of $1.55 are evidence of that belief. I hope that they will join the rest of us by agreeing to just a little less protection at the ceiling than they had tried to get.
May I add a word or two on the question of quantities. As further evidence that the proposed range of prices is reasonable under all the circumstances, requests were made for increases in their guaranteed quantities by many importing countries, adding up in total to very large amounts. Unfortunately, because of a series of short crops, Australia, on the exporting side, could not agree to maintain her quota and submitted a lower figure. It was, therefore, impossible to meet all the requests for increases by the importing countries. Canada, however, agreed to increase her guaranteed quantities from 235 million bushels, which applies during the final year of the present agreement, up to 250 million bushels for the three years of the new agreement. The agreement will relate to approximately 600 million bushels if all countries join. A guaranteed quantity for the United Kingdom is included at the present level of 177 million bushels.
The new agreement will come into force if signed by April 27 and accepted by July 15, 1953, by importers representing 50 per cent of the guaranteed quantities, and by exporters representing 50 per cent of the guaranteed quantities. There is provision for withdrawal by any exporting country if an important importing country fails to accept, and vice versa.
Wheat
May I add that throughput the negotiations the position taken by the Canadian delegation had the unanimous support of the five farm advisers-Messrs. Parker, Wesson, Plu-mer, Brownlee and Coates. The government is grateful to them for their assistance and their patience.
I cannot speak too highly of the work of Canada's three official delegates, M. W. Sharp, W. C. McNamara, and Dr. C. F. Wilson. Their skill as negotiators, their patience and industry, were in my opinion responsible for avoiding a breakdown in the lengthy negotiations. Their efforts to reconcile the conflicting views of the largest exporter with those of the largest importer were tireless and, I believe, effective to a high degree.
The present international wheat agreement is one of the few successful international commodity arrangements. The measure of its success is that the 46 member countries were willing to spend five weeks in London and ten weeks in Washington trying to agree on terms of renewal, and that they were almost able to reach unanimity in their final recommendations.
In the light of this success and these efforts, I think there is reason to be hopeful that the agreement will continue in full vigour for another three years. The Canadian government will leave no stone unturned to achieve that objective.

Mr. Speaker, I rise
merely for the purpose of asking one or two questions. I realize that the matter is not debatable at this time but I am sure Your Honour would raise no objection if I say that, in my opinion, the prices set will be disappointing to the expectations of the western farmers.
The questions I rise to ask are these. Does the minister believe that it will be possible to make an international wheat agreement either effective or even operative without the participation of Great Britain? Second, in the anticipated agreement is there any provision for escalator clauses to cover possible rises in the cost of production? Finally, will the minister say which were the importing countries that abstained from voting when the final determination as to prices was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first question is yes. The answer to the second question is no. The countries that abstained from voting were New Zealand, Greece, Ceylon and India.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question of the minister? Would he say whether he or some other minister would contemplate flying to Britain

Questions
within the next two weeks in order to see whether or not the British cabinet could be persuaded to sign this agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not customary to announce government policy in advance. If I do fly to England I will certainly let the house know after I return what transpired.

Mr. Speaker, there are two difficulties in the way of this notice of motion. One is a question of interpretation. If my hon. friend reads the notice of motion, I am sure he will realize that it is not clear. I do not know what he means by it. For instance, it is set out that there is required-
-a copy of all correspondence, letters, telegrams and other documents, since the first day of January, 1951, which have passed between any person or persons . . .
Then it goes on to deal with certain applications. This might mean that it were to cover correspondence between Mr. X in Regina and Mr. Y in Regina or Mr. X in Saskatoon and Mr. Y in Saskatoon. With all due respect to my hon. friend may I say that, if he will be good enough to couch the motion in one of the two official languages of this house, I shall be glad to see that he gets a reply. When he does indicate that the motion is one which I presume is directed at the Department of Transport, then may I say to him now, so there will be no loss -of time, that there is no objection to the motion as presumably reworded with this one exception, that all letters, correspondence, telegrams and so forth should, I take it, be produced with the exception of the application itself. It has been the policy not to produce the application, and for technical and financial reasons I take it that it should not be produced. I do not think my hon. friend will want that. Subject to that, I presume the order could go through.

Do I understand that the
motion is to be dropped and reworded or does it carry in its present form? I take it that the motion is to be dropped and reworded.
Agreed.
Motion dropped.

STRIKE OF GRAIN HANDLERS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FURTHER REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there have been reports over the radio and in the newspapers indicating that considerable activity has been taking place in connection with the negotiations with respect to the grain handlers, dispute on the west coast. Will the minister bring the house up to date?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STRIKE OF GRAIN HANDLERS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FURTHER REPORT
speechtext:
There is nothing of a definite nature that I can report to the house but perhaps I may be permitted to bring the house up to date

following the statement I made on the 24th of March, to be found at page 3230 of Hansard. I placed on record at that time the proposal which our chief conciliation officer, Mr. Wilson, had made to both parties with the object of effecting a settlement. No formal reply was received from either party until toward the end of last week. In the late afternoon of April 9 the following wire was received from Mr. R. H. Tupper on behalf of the employers. The wire is addressed to Mr. Bernard Wilson, chief conciliation officer, Department of Labour, and reads as follows:
Referring your letter March 20th regret delays arising from settlement of Port Arthur differences prevented earlier reply. Am directed by all five elevator companies concerned in dispute in Vancouver and New Westminster to inform you that they leave open their offer to grant two additional statutory holidays, an increase of 5 cents per hour in present graveyard shift differential, payment of double time for all work done on Sundays and to provide where practicable for proper job rotations provided the union will join with the companies in submitting as the only outstanding difference to be determined the question of wages for arbitration before a judge of the Appeal Court or Supreme Court of British Columbia.
On the next day, the 10th of April, the following wire was sent at 1.46 p.m. Pacific time by Mr. E. C. Sims on behalf of the unions. This wire reads as follows:
Re your wire April 9-
I should interject that the terms of the wire I have just read were conveyed to the unions. This wire is also addressed to Mr. Wilson. I continue:
-we note the companies have rejected your proposal of March 20th and submitted counter proposal re arbitration. I am instructed to inform you this counter proposal has been rejected and your March 20th proposal will be taken to membership tomorrow for acceptance or rejection. Will inform you of results.
On the next day, the 11th of April, the following wire, addressed to Mr. Wilson, was sent by Mr. Sims at 11.40 p.m. Pacific time:
Full general membership meeting held today. I am instructed to inform you that question put re acceptance or rejection of your proposal of arbitration dated March 20. Motion carried rejecting the proposal with twenty-nine dissenting votes. Results of vote indicate same strength as when strike vote taken. Manner of voting decided by motion of membership. Results indicate tie-up to go on indefinitely unless employers change attitude toward wage question and fringe benefits.
Since the receipt of these wires we have continued our efforts to bring the parties together for further negotiations. I can report nothing further this morning.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 228, to amend the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before third reading is given to this bill to amend the Income Tax Act there are one or two things I would like to say. In the first place I wish to say that this bill does nothing to narrow the tremendous gulf that exists in our income tax legislation between business and professional people on the one hand and the ordinary worker on the other.
I speak with particular reference to the matter of deductions or exemptions that are allowed to these two groups of taxpayers. This matter was particularly drawn to my attention, although I have spoken of it in

the house on previous occasions, when I received through the mail a few days ago a little vest pocket booklet entitled "Canadian Pocketax, 1953" which has been issued by the National Trust Company Limited, 250 Portage avenue, Winnipeg. It seems to me to be quite up to date and to take into consideration the changes being made this year in our income tax legislation. It is one of those little booklets that various firms sometimes put out to advise people as to their rights and privileges, as well as their obligations, under the Income Tax Act.
What interested me particularly, as I went through the pages of this little booklet, was to find that it takes more than four pages to list what are known as deductible items. The deductible items on these four pages are listed under a total of 46 main headings. If one were to break down these main categories into the subdivisions that are included he would find that the number is much larger. However, when one goes through these deductible items, and when one reads the preliminary paragraphs commenting on them, it becomes clear that this long list of deductions is not available to the ordinary worker when he files his income tax return.
The ordinary worker, as a matter of fact, finds himself for the most part limited to just four possible deductions, apart from his personal or family or statutory exemptions. Those four which are available to the ordinary worker, if he meets the required conditions, are:	Deduction for contributions
to an approved pension plan; deduction for allowable trade union dues; deduction for charitable donations; and a deduction for medical expenses, but only on that portion of expenses which exceed, from now on, 3 per cent of his gross income.
Beyond these four there are no deductions available to the average worker. In other words, when he gets his pay and when he is confronted with his income tax bill, he has had it. His tax, for the most part, is a tax on what he actually gets-and there is no fooling around with it. For the other group who are on what is called "gross income", whether it is because they operate a business or are in the various professions, there is, as I have pointed out, this long list of deductions which the National Trust Company has listed in this little book. I am not going to take the time of the house to read all of these forty-six main headings but I would like to name some of them. Here they are:	Accounting expenses; advertising
expenses; appraisal costs for insurance; bad debts; carrying charges; carting charges; efficiency experts' fees; industrial engineers' fees; insurance premiums; fire, theft and
Income Tax Act
group insurance premiums deductible by the employer; interest on borrowed money; interest on succession duties; legal expenses to collect past due debts, to defend actions under the Combines Investigation Act, and to protect the right to do business; production control costs; raw material costs; promotional expenses; secretarial expenses; taxes on real estate; cost of technical assistance; and telephone, and so on.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I have not read all of them but those are some of the main headings in this list of forty-six deductible items set out in this little booklet. It is very interesting to get this little book and to find that so many deductions are permitted, but it only draws attention to the tremendous gulf that this government's income tax legislation has established between the people who get their income in what is called a "gross form" on the one hand-business and professional people-and the ordinary working people who are on salary or receive a pay envelope on the other.
Of that list the latter taxpayer is limited to the four deductions I read out earlier. Incidentally, my colleague from Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) points out that a telephone is an essential to the earning of a livelihood in the case of many workers, such as railway men, who must have a telephone so that they can be called. But they do not get such a deduction. There are travelling expenses which are an essential part of the earning of a livelihood of many industrial workers, but for the industrial worker who is on wages they are not allowed. He gets none of these many deductions available to business and professional people. He is limited to the four which I have read, as anyone can see by referring to the short income tax form. He gets his deduction for a pension plan, provided it has been approved by the department; some are and some are not. He gets his trade union dues allowed, provided those dues are for the purposes spelled out in the act. He gets charitable donations allowed, up to a certain amount, provided he has the receipts. There are many instances where charitable donations are made by individuals who are unable to get receipts for them. As for medical expenses, of course, he gets only those expenses that are set out in the act, and he gets only that portion in excess of 3 per cent of his gross income.
Now, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is a serious matter and that something should be done to narrow that gulf. If the minister is not prepared to widen and extend the exemptions that are allowed to the ordinary worker, I submit that he should apply the

Income Tax Act
axe to many of those deductions and exemptions that are allowed to that other group. Surely, the one principle that should characterize our income tax legislation is fairness. Here is a place where unfairness persists, and I strongly urge the minister to reconsider this whole question. This is not the first time I have made this appeal to the minister, but I point out that there has been no narrowing of this gulf in the legislation presented this year. In fact, some of the so-called technical changes in the bill now before us have actually widened that gulf, for they extend still greater concessions to those on the business or professional side of the picture.
I remind the minister again of a particular example of this unfairness which has to do with the fact that the government has, as yet, done nothing about the ruling of the income tax appeal board to the effect that the expenses of lawyers attending conventions of the bar association are deductible. The minister has said this is a matter for the courts to decide. I remind the minister that when the courts have made decisions on other matters that were at variance with what the government had intended the legislation to provide, they have changed the legislation so as to make it conform to what they originally intended. I could cite other cases, but I shall stick to income tax matters;'.
The minister remembers the Bond and Rutherford case back in 1946, when Mr. Justice Thorson of the exchequer court ruled that the fees of those two lawyers to the law society were to be allowed as deductible, even though they were on a net salary rather than on gross income. It was very interesting to note that, in that particular case, no action was taken by the government to change the law to meet what had been their original intention. In that instance lawyers were involved, but a few years later another judge of the same exchequer court, Mr. Justice Angers, ruled that the same right to deduct fees paid to an association should be extended to trade unions, and the government immediately amended both the old income war tax act and the Income Tax Act so as to make the law read the way they had intended in the first place. The government simply said that they recognized the decision by the exchequer court as indicating what the law meant as it was then written, but they did not mean that so they changed the law to make it read the way they intended. Fortunately, that chapter has a much brighter sequel in that the government was later persuaded to change the law to grant the right of deductibility in respect of trade union dues.

But then we come to the case of Mr. Parkinson, the lawyer who claimed deductibility for his expenses in attending a convention of the bar association. He made out his income tax form including those expenses as a deductible item, but the department rejected his claim. I think it is fair to assume that the department knew what the government intended. As soon as Mr. Parkinson had his claim denied by the Department of National Revenue, he took his case to the income tax appeal board, which board acts now in these cases instead of the exchequer court. Mr. W. S. Fisher, Q.C., of the income tax appeal board, ruled that as the law read Mr. Parkinson, even though he was on a salary, had the right to deduct his expenses to the convention of the bar association. Surely that is a case where it is quite clear that the income tax appeal board has ruled that the law says something different from what the government intended it to mean. What happened back in Mr. Cooper's case with regard to trade union dues? Actually the same thing, and when that happened, the government changed the law to make it say what they intended it to mean. But now in the case of Mr. Parkinson and the expenses of lawyers attending the bar association when a corresponding judicial body says that the law means something the government never intended it to mean, the government refuses to take any action.
I submit that in all fairness the government should do one or the other of two things. Either they should amend the law so as to permit deductibility for expenses to conventions to be extended to all trade unionists, farmers, those attending church conventions, school teachers and all the rest, or they should amend the law to make it clear that lawyers do not have that particular right. I have no particular quarrel with my lawyer friends in the house, some of whom are staring at me while I am making these remarks. As a matter of fact, I believe most of them will agree with me, whether or not they are personally affected, that there should be fairness in respect of this matter.

I do not know whether the
hon. member was referring to me as one of the lawyers who were staring, but if so the reason I was staring at him was that I was rather concerned about whether he was in order. As the hon. member knows, on third reading of a bill a member can discuss only what is in the bill. He cannot go beyond the bill as it is presented for third reading. It seems to me he is getting away from the bill as presented to the house for third reading.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I want to say at the outset
that I was not referring to you, sir, as one of the lawyers who were staring at me. I shall not go so far as to name the ones to whom I referred, but may I just say that it did seem to me that on third reading it was proper to deal with the general principle of this bill. However, I assure Your Honour that I have said all I need to say on that particular subject. I feel I should point out that this bill amends the Income Tax Act, and some of its changes involve widening the exemptions and the deductible items that are provided in the Income Tax Act. I was expressing my regret-if Your Honour feels I have gone far enough, I shall leave it at that-that at a time when changes were being made in the provisions for deductibility, the government had not seen fit to make the necessary change to clear up this injustice, this inequity. During the course of the debate, when we were in committee of the whole on the bill, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said in a number of instances that the reason for the point he was introducing was to clear up an inequity or an injustice. Well, I have cited what I regard as a gross inequity, a gross injustice, and I hope that one of these days soon it will be cleared up.
I leave that item as I have put it, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest that it is another example of the case I was making earlier, namely, that there is too wide a gulf between the treatment accorded by the Income Tax Act, as we are now amending it, to the business and professional groups on the one hand and to the ordinary workers on salary on the other.
There is just one other comment I wish to make and then I shall take my seat. I do this very briefly; I do it by no means in any argumentative tone but rather just to place my position on the record with respect to it. Earlier in this session, in connection with one of the taxation bills, the Minister of Finance, not on a point of order and yet with reference to a matter of procedure, expressed the view that it was proper to precede a taxation bill with a resolution much shorter in form than that to which we are accustomed. In fact, he said it was now his view that it was not necessary, in the resolution preceding a taxation bill, to spell out the proposed changes. He said that all that was necessary was to bring in a resolution saying that it is expedient to amend such and such a bill. The Minister of Finance did not contend that he was going to change the practice now being followed, and I am sure that he does not intend to do so. I am sure that for his .purposes the 68108-238
Income Tax Act
present practice of presenting resolutions which give a certain amount of detail is much more satisfactory. Because I am sure he has no such intention I do not wish to argue the point; I simply wish to say this. I have secured the memorandum on this matter to which the Minister of Finance referred the other day, and which he invited us to secure, and I must say-and this is the point that I wish to put on the record- that in my view the memorandum is well put with respect to another matter, but it does not deal with this point at all. It is a memorandum on the question as to whether or not a resolution preceding a money bill should stipulate the maximum amount of money to be included in that bill. That is a different question altogether in my humble but very considered opinion.
The memorandum to which the minister refers really does not deal with the point he was speaking about the other day, and since it does not deal with it, it does not back up his case in the way that he seemed to feel it did. Now, I am not going to go into it in any detail; I am not going to argue the point, but I simply felt that the minister having said what he did the other day I should report that I have read the memorandum, and that, in my view, it would be very difficult for him to make a case on it for the proposition that he gave the house. I leave it at that because I am satisfied, as I have already said, there is no intention to change the practice; that it is more satisfactory for the minister as well as for the house as a whole to follow the present practice of bringing in, prior to taxation bills, resolutions that give us a fair amount of detail as to what is to be expected in the bills themselves.

I
should like to make one or two brief comments. In the first place I should like to associate myself with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has just said. I was surprised at the breadth of the statement made by the minister the other day, but I do not propose to deal with it because I think in fact that in practice we shall find that the minister does not go the length which that statement might be presumed to take us.
This bill is like the curate's egg, Mr. Speaker. It is good in parts and therefore we are not going to propose an amendment; nor shall we oppose the bill. There are certain things in it which we have approved again and again, namely, the reduction of the income tax on persons and corporations. But on the other hand I wish very briefly to reiterate the fact that there are certain things

Income Tax Act
in the bill which we have disapproved and which we still disapprove. I wish to maintain that position to the end.
We are not able to bring about any alterations in these, but we have of course continued to disapprove of the fact that the sales tax has been unaltered. We have pointed out that it means the great bulk of the people benefit very little from the present budget. We sought to have relief given to municipalities and school boards on their purchases, but that is denied us. Mr. Speaker, that is all I wish to say.

I am
going to be very brief. I intended to say a few words on second reading, but the hon. gentleman who has just spoken failed to take part in the debate on second reading and it passed before I realized it.
We in this group regret this Income Tax Act still provides for the income taxation of cooperatives. We believe that co-operatives are the economic hope of the world, and we think that the government would be doing a great service to this country if they would eliminate those sections in the act that provide for the taxation of co-operatives. In that respect I am going to be quite brief because I realize a good deal of time has been spent on this bill. I do want to quote what Canon Coady had to say in this respect:
It has been said that nature is red in tooth and claw. This is the philosophy of the survival of the fittest, but it is fundamentally erroneous. Cooperation, more than competition, is the chief factor in survival. Nature at its best is co-operative. We see it in the human family, the primary unit of society.
Co-operative nations can make the world a family. There is here the germ of universal peace. Until this foundation is laid for peace, there is not much hope for the future.
This excerpt is taken from "Social Significance of the Co-operative Movement".
We believe exactly as the canon does in that respect. A large number of my constituents are very concerned about the income taxation of co-operatives. We were very sorry indeed that the government decided, shall I say, to surrender to the views of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, who presented a brief to the royal commission on co-operatives in 1945, and to illustrate its point of view I want to quote from that brief. It was an excellent brief from the chamber's point of view. It dealt with the position of co-operatives so far as taxation is concerned, and in one paragraph it said this in part:
After a slow rate of growth over many decades the rapid expansion of co-operatives and mutuals in Canada has been substantially enhanced by their exemption from liability for income taxation. The record supports that conclusion. While this position of special privilege is maintained the

expansion of co-operative and mutual associations will continue, leading finally to the removal of a considerable part of the commerce of the country from the taxable to the tax-exempt form of business organization.
From the point of view of the business interests, that is a sound analysis of the situation. However, we in this group believe that the co-operative movement is a movement that should be supported in every way possible and that this government could not assist such a movement to better advantage than by removing the income taxation of co-operatives at this time.
While we agree with various deductions made for travel expenses in the act, before taking my seat I do want to bring to the attention of the house and the minister again the fact that we believe that workers who have to live some distance away from their employment, up to thirty to thirty-five miles, are put to abnormal expenses of from $10 to $25 a month, which they often cannot afford, and should be permitted to deduct these expenses for income tax purposes. In addition to that, we in this group believe that not only should oil companies, gas companies and mining companies receive exemption on developing properties, but that farmers who are clearing land, who are bringing land into production, should be allowed to deduct these expenses for income tax purposes. In that connection we support the proposal of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which in its presentation to the cabinet this year said, on the subject of tax exemption on clearing and breaking:
In our opinion it is desirable to encourage the improvement and development of our farm lands, just as much as it is to encourage the exploration and development of minerals and oil by special inducements. We therefore recommend that clearing, breaking and improving of farm lands be deductible as a farm expense where such acreages are reasonable in relation to the general farm operation.
We support that point of view, and regret a provision is not made for those deductions in the bill.
Finally, while I agree with the minister that there are administrative difficulties, and that possibly there have been some abuses on the part of some provincial governments, I think due consideration should be given to the removal of the sales tax from supplies, equipment and machines purchased by municipalities.
I think that question was discussed previously under another bill.

Perhaps so; I am just concluding what I have to say. I do think the violations of the law could be overcome by strict regulations.

speechtext:
Yes, it has been circulated. It is Bill No. 331.
At this time there is very little that I can add to what I said on that occasion; I think, however, I should remind hon. members that for some time it has been becoming more and more apparent that, owing to the increasing ramifications of the work of the board, its structure required some modifications. The modifications which the amendments will bring about will permit wider regional representation on the board itself. This will permit representation from Newfoundland and additional representation from central Canada.
Under the present set-up the chairman and the vice-chairman are professors doing university work in Queen's and Toronto universities respectively. It is thought desirable that the chairman should be a full-time scientist residing at Ottawa. This will permit of continuous attention to the management and co-ordination of work done at the various stations. The chairman will be responsible for seeing that the program laid down by the board at the annual meeting is carried out.
The work of the board has grown tremendously over the years. A decade ago the budget of the board amounted to approximately one-quarter of a million dollars. Today it is close to the two million mark. It is apparent, therefore, that the chairman should be located at headquarters in Ottawa so that greater co-ordination can exist between the various stations and the Department of Fisheries.
When this bill was in the resolution stage the hon. member for St. John's West asked me if there would be representation from the province of Newfoundland on the board. One of the purposes of the amendments is to permit of such representation.

speechtext: Will the minister give us an explanation?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing the resolution I believe I can make the statement that this country is justly proud of the legislation it has put on the statute books for the benefit of its veterans, which legislation has come to be known as the veterans charter. I can also state that all members of the House of Commons, irrespective of party

affiliation, have looked upon veterans legislation in years past in a generous and unselfish way, in a manner truly reminiscent of the high spirit of service of those who enlisted in the Canadian forces.
As was stated once by one of my predecessors, the Hon. Ian Mackenzie, the veterans charter grew in spirit, substance and final form out of the hearts and minds of a united people dedicating themselves and the lives of their sons and daughters to victory. Its basic provisions were the result of a desire to deal in a just manner with all who served.
In view of what I have just said, I am confident that all members of the House of Commons will welcome the introduction at this time of a measure to provide assistance for the higher education of children of certain deceased members of the armed forces and other persons. As the committee will recall, the legislation governing rehabilitation for world war II veterans provided assistance in a training program designed to fit the veteran into suitable employment. It provided training assistance for the veteran with little formal schooling at one end of the scale and right up to university graduation at the other. The purpose of this resolution is to assist financially pensioned sons and daughters of former members of the forces, who have died as a result of service, in obtaining post-secondary education.
Such a program has been under consideration by the department for some time, and the time has now come when many of these children are reaching university age. I might add that it is also proposed to extend the benefits to be derived from the terms of the legislation to children of Canadian veterans who have lost their lives as the result of service in Korea.
For the information of the house I might say that at the present time there are approximately 12,000 children who are receiving pensions under schedule B of the Pension Act. An analysis made by the department shows that the peak load of candidates for the type of training that this legislation will provide for those whose fathers served in world war II will come between 1958 and 1962. Candidates who qualify under the act will receive a training allowance during the time they are in full time intramural attendance plus payment of their tuition fees. In addition to occupations for which graduation from university is required there are occupations, as hon. members know, for which high school graduation -that is matriculation or the equivalent of university admission-is required. Teacher training, through the provincial normal

schools, and nursing, through the teaching hospitals, are cases in point. Under the Veterans Rehabilitation Act which provided training to world war II veterans these latter were classified as "vocational". The bill is designed to provide assistance in these training institutions for which high school graduation, matriculation that is, is now a prerequisite.
The provincially controlled secondary schools, that is the high school, technical and commercial schools, provide training required for entry into the most common occupations. Statistics indicate that some 60 per cent of young people entering high school leave without completing the usual four-year program, and not more than 10 per cent or about one-quarter of those who do graduate proceed, or are likely to proceed, with further schooling-post-secondary education.
The bill which will follow this resolution is designed to deal with this latter group eligible for admission and seeking admission to training institutions for which high school graduation is required. In other words, the criterion is secondary school graduation- regardless of whether the proposed occupation requirement is regarded as university or vocational.
That, Mr. Chairman, constitutes the general outline of the proposed measure and I shall be glad, when we are in committee on the bill, to go into any further details-for instance, questions of eligibility, type of education contemplated, benefits available, academic standing required and time limits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes certain amendments to the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act, 1937, as amended. The principal objects of this bill are four in number: the first object is found under section 2 of the bill where provision is made to increase the number of directors of Trans-Canada Air Lines from seven to nine persons. This will enable a wider geographical representation on the board of directors.
The second object is seen in section 9, subsections 1, 2 and 3 which provide for a rearrangement of the capital structure of the corporation to bring it in line with the normal commercial practice of financing part of the corporation's undertakings by means of equity capital and part by borrowed money.
Under these provisions Canadian National Railway Company will be required to surrender 200,000 shares of the capital stock of the corporation for a bond or debenture having a face value of $20 million, bearing a fixed interest rate and payable at a definite time in the future.
In this connection since the inception of Trans-Canada Air Lines the practice has been followed of requiring the air line to pay to the railway company interest on the railway company's investment in the air line. This principle was written into the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act, 1937, during what was called in the act the "initial period". During

the initial period the air line was permitted to add to its operating expenses five per cent on the capital invested in the air line and deficits, if any, were made up by upward revisions of mail payments to the corporation by the department of the Postmaster General. The initial period was to end on December 31, 1939, but was extended by parliament on two occasions and finally came to an end on March 31, 1942. Since April 1, 1948, interest on the capital invested has been paid by the air line to the railway company at the rate of 3 per cent per annum.
The third object of the bill relates to income tax liability. The rearrangement of the financial structure of the corporation will have the effect of keeping the income tax liability of Trans-Canada Air Lines within normal commercial limits. If the capital structure were allowed to remain in the form of equity capital only, no deduction from that income would be permitted for income tax purposes on the interest payment hitherto paid or to be paid to the railway company, with the result that the railway company might be forced to look for payment by way of return on its investment to the net earnings of the corporation, if any, after payment of income tax. Furthermore, the provisions of subsection 4 of section 9 propose to give legal effect for income tax purposes to the interest paid to the railway company on the capital invested during the calendar year 1952 and, as well, up to the time of enactment of the bill, limited to three per cent on the capital invested by the railway company in the air line.
The fourth object of the bill is to be found in section 20. This provides for the extinction of the company incorporated under the name "Trans-Canada Air Lines (Atlantic) Limited." This company was formed to take over the responsibilities and activities of a wartime organization known as the Canadian government transatlantic air service. That organization was set up for the primary purpose of providing a rapid mail service to Canadian troops serving overseas, and its operation was made the responsibility of Trans-Canada Air Lines. When the Canadian government transatlantic air service was discontinued, it was thought desirable to form a separate company to continue overseas operations. There no longer seems to be any reason for making a corporate distinction between what are in effect two divisions of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and the absorption of Trans-Canada Air Lines (Atlantic) Limited into the parent company, Trans-Canada Air Lines, has many administrative advantages.
The above are the principal objects of the bill. However, there are some minor objects. There are certain proposed amendments in
13, 1953
Trans-Canada Air Lines Act section 1 of the bill to section 2 of the act, which might be termed "clean-up" amendments, as they remove from this section definitions of words or expressions which are no longer referred to in the act.
By section 3 of the bill, subsection 3 of section 7 is amended by providing that Canadian National Railway Company may sell the shares of the capital stock of the corporation only with the approval of parliament.
By section 5 of the bill, section 13 of the act is amended to provide that the auditor appointed by parliament to audit the accounts of Canadian National Railway Company will be the auditor of Trans-Canada Air Lines instead of an auditor appointed by the minister.
By section 6 of the bill, certain amendments are made to section 14 of the act which authorize Trans-Canada Air Lines to carry out functions directly connected with the operation of the air line. This section also authorizes Trans-Canada Air Lines to use the descriptive name "Air Canada" which already has wide recognition in the Frenchspeaking sections of the country.
By section 8 of the bill, section 20 of the act is repealed by providing that if another corporation is formed under the provisions of section 20, the number of directors shall not exceed nine, instead of seven as presently provided in section 20.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks to make at this time, and I shall ask some questions when we get into committee, and are discussing the sections of the bill. My observations at this time will be general.
I can understand the reasons the minister has given. The desire to escape taxation is one of the most human desires, and apparently it exists even in crown corporations. The reason the minister has given is quite understandable.
I should like to reiterate briefly something that took place in the debate on the resolution, because I think it is a matter of some importance. I had asked the minister a question with regard to the monopoly position of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and I should like to read my question and the minister's answer, because I regard his answer as of sufficient importance to have it on the record.
As reported at page 3548 of Hansard I asked this question:
I would like to ask the minister a question having regard to the answer he gave to the member for Winnipeg North Centre.
That was in answer to a quotation the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had read from a statement by Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Trans-Canada Air Lines Act King on April 2, 1943, which seemed to indicate almost that the monopoly position was going to be without end, or at least there was no indication of an end. I asked this question:
We do have competition between the railways, and I believe they feel it is good. The chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation spoke about the usefulness of competition. I wanted to ask the minister whether the policy enunciated by Mr. King might not be changed, and whether we might not reasonably look forward to a time when there would be enough airplane traffic for more than one company.
To that the minister replied:
The hon. member is quite right. This is a thinly settled country. We have air services that are essential to the economy. However, today air transport in Canada is not competitive, or is competitive in only a few cases, whether public or private. If an air line company is assigned to a territory, that is its territory and no one else has a right to operate an air service in it. I believe that is a sound policy at the moment. If sufficient travel develops to the point where competition is warranted, then certainly air routes may be entitled to competition.
Having put that on the record, I shall reserve anything I have to say until we reach the sections of the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 100, to prevent discrimination in regard to employment and membership in trade unions by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this bill for second reading I should like to make a few remarks. The speech from the throne last December declared the government's intention to introduce a bill which would prohibit discrimination in employment against any person because of his race, national origin, colour or religion in connection with any work, undertaking or business within the legislative authority of parliament. National labour organizations and many other bodies in recent years have advocated such federal legislation.
I think it is only fair to say that several members of the house have stressed the importance of the government taking some action in this field. I do feel that it would be wrong in introducing the bill if I did not acknowledge one voice from this side of the house that has been forceful, consistent and eloquent in its demands for action against discrimination for many more years than I have been a member of the house. I refer of course to the voice of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I wish to express to him my warmest thanks for all he has done in the past to help prepare the ground to make possible the introduction of this bill at this time. I am sure there are many Canadians
3762	HOUSE OF
Fair Employment Practices outside the house who would want me to make this public expression of gratitude to the hon. member for Spadina on their behalf.
Also, it is with respect that I acknowledge the sponsorship of similar private members' bills by the official opposition labour critic, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). It was very kind of her to withdraw her bill from the order paper this year to make way for mine, and I welcome her support of the principle of the bill.
I believe that equality of opportunity for employment without discrimination on account of race, national origin, colour or religion is a fundamental right which every resident of our democratic state should enjoy. It is a right which this parliament can well assert and try to protect. The government is now asking parliament to make this assertion by the bill I am introducing in respect of all persons in Canada who are employed or seeking employment in activities which come under federal authority. Although this federal sphere of jurisdiction is relatively limited, I believe that the passing of this legislation may have a far-reaching and healthy influence across the whole country.
I think one can say that the underlying principle of the bill is assurance of equality of vocational opportunity. In recent years Canada, as a member of various international organizations, has subscribed to general declarations concerning the basic rights and liberties of the individual. However, because of the divided jurisdiction established by our federal constitution, Canadian representatives have not always been able to make specific commitments with regard to legislation to ensure the protection of human rights.
For example, in 1948 the Canadian delegation to the general assembly of the United Nations voted for the universal declaration of human rights which was adopted by the assembly on December 10 of that year. The head of our delegation stated that certain important aspects of the declaration lay within the field of provincial jurisdiction in Canada and that the federal government did not intend to invade that field. Canadian participation in the international labour organization has been affected in the same way by the federal nature of our constitution. Canadian delegates to the general conference of the ILO in 1944 approved the adoption of the new declaration of the aims of the ILO which became known afterwards as the Philadelphia charter. This declaration asserts, among other things, the solemn obligation of the ILO to promote among the nations of the world programs which will achieve full employment, higher standards of living, the


extension of social security, adequate protection for the life and health of workers, effective recognition of the right of collective bargaining-and this is the one that embraces the principle of this bill-equality of vocational opportunity, and other conditions conducive to human well-being.
Some action has already been taken by this government to prevent discrimination in employment in those areas of jurisdiction within which the federal authority has power to legislate.
At the last session the Unemployment Insurance Act was amended to provide that it is the duty of the commission to ensure that there will be no discrimination in referring any worker seeking employment, either in favour of or against any such worker, by reason of his racial origin, colour, religious belief or political affiliation. Then, as a further step in its program, in September last an order in council was passed which requires the insertion of a non-discrimination clause in federal government construction and supplies contracts entered into on or after January 1, 1953, to which the government fair wage provisions apply.
This clause expressly forbids the contractor to discriminate against any person because of his race, national origin, colour or religion in the employment of labour for the execution of the contract.
It might be said that discrimination in employment is based on ignorance, prejudice, selfishness, or an attitude of mind which cannot be discovered or changed by legislation. I agree, Mr. Speaker, that there is much to be said for that view. However, I would like to stress the point that the legislation which I am introducing is designed to deal with positive acts of discrimination. There will still be need for continued effort on the part of all those educational, religious, cultural, yes, and government influences, which are now working together and doing so much to create in Canada a climate of opinion in which racial and religious prejudice shall find no place.
The provisions of the legislation will apply to all employers of five or more employees, excluding non-profit educational, fraternal, charitable, religious and social organizations. The legislation applies to employment upon any work, undertaking or business which is within the legislative authority of parliament to regulate, to crown companies, and to trade unions composed of persons employed upon such works, undertakings or businesses. In effect, the legislation applies in respect of the same industries to which the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act applies.
The provisions of the bill will prohibit employers from discrimination as defined

against any person in respect of employment or prospective employment, and prohibits employers from using the services of any employment agency which in its operations so discriminates against persons seeking employment. The use of advertising in connection with employment which expresses any such discrimination or preference is prohibited. Trade unions shall not so discriminate against any person in the matter of membership.
The legislation will be administered by the Department of Labour and by a division of the work amongst existing staff. It is not anticipated that additional costs for administration will be great.
Provision is made in the legislation for the receipt and investigation of complaints by conciliation officers of the department, and for the use of industrial inquiry commissions for the purpose of ascertaining the facts, with a view to the adjustment of complaints made under the act. Provision is made for prosecution in the courts for alleged infractions of the act and for the imposition of penalties by way of fine and recovery of lost wages where the offence is proved. This procedure for the handling and disposition of complaints is very similar to the procedures provided under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act for the handling and disposition of complaints of unfair labour practices. It is proposed to use the same administrative machinery.
I believe that legislation of this nature to deal with overt acts of discrimination is practical and can be administered. The record of New York state, which pioneered in the United States in prohibiting discrimination against workers, has established the effectiveness of an act of this kind.
Passed in 1945, the New York law set a pattern for similar laws in ten other states and, I think, for the fair employment practices act enacted by the province of Ontario in 1951. Experience under the Ontario act perhaps has been of too limited duration to permit an adequate appraisal of its effectiveness. But there is ample evidence that in 71 years of its operation the New York law has had an appreciable effect in eliminating discrimination and in broadening job opportunities' for minority groups.
Briefly stated, the New York law provides that no person shall be denied the right to earn a living because of his religious belief or his racial or national background. It lays down penalties for acts of discrimination, whether by employers, labour organizations, employment agencies or other individuals.
The term "employer" under the New York act does not include a non-profit organization
Fair Employment Practices or an employer with fewer than six persons in his employ. The act does not apply to a person employed by his parent, spouse or child, nor to domestic servants.
While punitive powers are provided for the New York act, to be used when and if needed, the policy of the commission administering the legislation has been to rely on conciliation and persuasion and to avoid legal proceedings wherever possible. The record shows that out of approximately 2,500 cases handled to date the New York commission has had to resort to court action only three times. When one considers this experience in that highly industrialized state it seems a great victory for conciliation and persuasion, with the teeth of the law almost entirely unused.
One might sum up by quoting the following paragraph from the commission's 1951 report on its administration of the law:
The commission realizes full well that the problems of employment discrimination which made a law necessary have not been completely solved. It is satisfied, however, that the law is no longer viewed by the general public as an expedient, an experiment, or a controversial document, but as an important instrument in the building of a stronger, democratic state.
The Ontario act has been in force since the middle part of 1951, and I am advised that in the intervening period, while there have been a limited number of complaints dealt with under the act, these complaints have been adjusted under the provisions of the act without the necessity of resort to the courts in any instance.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the principle of this bill will have wholehearted support in this house and amongst the citizens of this country. It is only with this large measure of public support that it will be effective for the purposes for which it is designed.
Following a discussion of the bill on second reading, if it is the wish of the house, I shall move to refer it for study to the standing committee on industrial relations. I am confident that it can be made into an effective ally to the main effort in Canada for ensuring equality of vocational opportunity.
It is as an -ally that I view this measure. The main effort against discrimination must continue to be carried on by individual Canadians with the potent weapons of human understanding, of charitable example, and with the application of the golden rule. If this bill becomes law we will see to it that it is used only to augment those weapons.
I commend it to the house.

speechtext:
I should like to join with the minister, Mr. Speaker, in paying tribute to the hon. member

Fair Employment Practices for Spadina (Mr. Croll) for the work which all of us know he has done in this field over a period of many years.
