I think that possibly at this time I might review some of the reasons for my support of this type of legislation and the motives which prompted me, in the first instance, to introduce a bill which, as the minister has said, I withdrew earlier in this session.
As I said on previous occasions, I think it is important that legislation should be provided to implement the universal declaration of human rights as proclaimed before the general assembly of the United Nations on December 10, 1948. Like the bill which it was my privilege to sponsor earlier, this bill applies only to employment in those fields which fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government. I am sure that every member of parliament will be in sympathy with the enactment of legislation which seeks to establish a common basis for all peoples in this nation, regardless of their origin, their religion or the various circumstances and conditions under which they labour. Canada is a nation of producers, and their production falls into many and varied categories. The very life and future of this nation depends upon those who, by their labours in every field, are building an economic stability to support a growing importance of international scope.
Quite apart from humanitarian standards, it is important that all citizens of Canada should recognize equality of effort which every day enhances our nationhood. It will be said, and truly so, that discrimination is of the heart and that legislation cannot alter the thoughts of man. But it is true also in other fields that all legislation sets a standard to which citizens tend to conform more and more as time goes on. In the past two years we have gone a long way towards recognition of the universality of human rights, and it is my opinion it is now expedient to put upon the statutes of this nation testimony to our belief in that fundamental principle. Of course, the members of my party propose to support this motion.
The preliminary steps in this direction which have already been taken were described by the minister, that is the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act and just latterly P.C. 4138 which became effective January 1 of this year with regard to government contracts. These steps, taken with the support of all members in this house as well as with the support of various labour organizations, have come about as a result of changing opinions, or perhaps I should say a realization on the part of the people that


there must come a time when we would put upon the statute books of this nation some tangible evidence of our belief in the equality of all citizens. I was very much interested some time ago in reading a statement which was submitted to the minister by the Canadian Congress of Labour, and I should like to quote two or three excerpts from it. The first one reads as follows:
The congress asserts that the denial of a job to any Canadian for no other reason than that his race, his creed, his colour or his ancestry is not that of the majority, is a violation of one of the most fundamental tenets of democracy: equality of opportunity. Such discrimination has no scientific basis; it is based- wholly on prejudice. It is contrary to the religious and moral values on which this country was founded.
Then a little later on the statement says:
It deprives Canada of the best efforts of countless thousands of her people and leaves her the poorer for it.
Then, touching upon the manner in which such legislation should operate, the statement says this:
The removal of prejudice is a long, hard task, and fair employment practices legislation is but one of the many means which must be used in the process.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the goal will not be reached overnight. Deeply held opinions and long practised habits are not easily changed. It is my opinion that lasting results can only be achieved by constant educational efforts, coupled with prompt and intelligent handling of reported situations. As the minister has said, this is a fairly new type of legislation. So far as I know the New York and New Jersey legislation of 1945 was about the first, and possibly the New York legislation has become a pattern for most of the -legislation which exists today. Because of that it is very easy to examine the New York record and to judge the effectiveness of such legislation by the experiences within that state. It was, therefore, very interesting to read the current report of the New York commission covering the year 1952. In the introduction, I find this paragraph, which I should like to read to the house:
The New York state law against discrimination, which started out on July 1, 1945 as an experiment in enlightened social legislation, may now be assessed, almost eight years later, as an essential statutory device in eradicating those practices of discrimination which not only deny individual interests and inventives, rights and privileges, but retard the growth of our economy by the squandering of our manpower resources. Such practices can never be justified in a democratic society, and to the extent that they continue to exist . . . they not only violate the law, but they tend to keep us from the immediate goal of our national defence production program: the most effective use of our available manpower supply. They also, quite obviously, supply grist for the propaganda mills of

those forces which seek to undermine the faith of . . . the people ... in our democratic form of government.
Then they, too, proceed to speak of the necessity for an educational program in connection with this type of legislation. A little further on they say this:
In 1945, when the law became effective, it was generally recognized that the ultimate goal could not be reached overnight. Although that observation is as valid today, it is the fact that persons formerly barred by reasons of discrimination from jobs in certain fields or prevented from advancing above menial or segregated levels of employment, have made definite progress towards the achievement of equal employment opportunity. The patterns of the past, however, are not easily changed, and a sizeable job remains to be done.
I was interested, Mr. Speaker, in the minister's remark that the implementation of this bill will be undertaken by the existing staff within his department. I was particularly interested in that because I had previously examined the estimates of the labour department, and I found no item especially earmarked for administration of this legislation. Therefore, possibly I can be forgiven if I wondered whether or not it was the government's intention to proceed very vigorously along the lines of administration of a Fair Employment Practices Act.
Now that the minister has made that explanation I should like to say this: I do hope that the government is not going to pass this bill and push it to one side, waiting for someone who happens to find out about it to make a complaint under the legislation. I believe that the full effectiveness of this legislation can only materialize if the government will institute a proper program of education to go hand in hand with the administration of the legislation itself. I believe that very strongly. We are all human, and we know that workers hesitate to make complaints, particularly those who are in menial employment. In many cases they are afraid of their jobs. They need to be assured that under this legislation it is their right to complain, but not to file complaints indiscriminately. Where there is definite basis for belief that they have been discriminated against they should be encouraged to make known instances and circumstances of such discrimination. I believe that, by removing from them the fear of retribution from employers or others, legislation of this sort can be made properly effective.
In this bill, as in the Ontario bill, provision is made for an industrial inquiry commission to look into such complaints as are made. This of course is an entirely different matter from a standing administrative commission or body to plan not only the administration but the education of workers in this field.
Fair Employment Practices I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to the establishment of a commission which will be charged with this responsibility. 1 feel that it would not only be a good thing at the federal level to have someone actively engaged in dissemination of information, but it would provide a stimulus to those provinces which have legislation of this order at the present time or who may, I hope, enact such legislation at a later date, to proceed along those lines. I believe that at the present time in the Dominion of Canada only two provinces, Saskatchewan and Ontario, have legislation of this kind. I understand that Manitoba is seriously considering such legislation, and one other was mentioned to me as being keenly interested in this type of legislation.
There should be a permanent administra-' tive body charged with this responsibility, and the establishment of a commission should not depend upon the receipt of complaints which cannot be handled by the ordinary conciliation officers of the department.
The minister has spoken of the limited experience which the province of Ontario has had in this matter, and that is quite true. It is my understanding that in the approximately two years that the act has been operative only ten complaints have been received, and these have all been easily handled. While the province of Ontario did not set up any educational program, it did cover the ground fairly thoroughly in the first instance with letters and information to employers, trade unions, and so on. A great deal can be done to make effective the provisions of this legislation if one specific body is definitely charged with this responsibility. This is the least we can do to make such legislation operative. If we are not going to go that far, then the enactment of such legislation is merely giving lip service to a principle; and while that is all very well in itself, unless we are prepared to take more active steps, the legislation itself cannot achieve the result that is desired. I feel very strongly upon this point, because I have travelled pretty extensively across this country and throughout the northern part of the United States. I have seen conditions under which a great many people work and I have witnessed all too frequently instances of discrimination which should not exist. It is up to those who have very definite opinions on this subject to voice them, and to voice them in places where they will be heard right across the length and breadth of this land.
We are creatures of habit. A great deal of the discrimination which exists today is merely habit. We are inclined to gather

Fair Employment Practices together in groups of our own kind, and that is true of those who come from other countries as well. We are proud of the traditions of our own particular race. We all suffer to some extent, and in varying degrees, from religious bigotry. Some of this we do not take seriously; some we do. Because we are human and given to human frailty it is necessary that we should dig beneath the surface of habits which produce discrimination and to set up this example of the intention of the people of this country so that discrimination cannot threaten the rights and privileges of the citizens of Canada, nor can it menace the institutions and foundations of a free democratic state.
Since this bill is to go to the committee on industrial relations I do not propose to speak on any particular clause thereof. There will be plenty of opportunity to discuss them in the committee, and later when we get to the committee stage in this house. In closing these few remarks on the principle of this bill, I should like to quote a small paragraph which has come to me and which is anonymous:
When people are no longer willing to help right the wrongs of others, their own rights are no longer safe.
And so, Mr. Speaker, in supporting this bill I say that if we are motivated by no more than selfishness, it behooves all members of this house to give their wholehearted support to the enactment of this legislation which will do away with one blight which unfortunately infests the whole North American continent today, and in so doing we shall support Canadian principles and give impetus to production, which this country needs more than anything else to take it farther along the road of progress on which it has so well started.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at once on behalf of the C.C.F. that we support the principle of this legislation. Indeed, I think in days to come it will be recognized that this bill has been something of a landmark in Canadian labour history. We believe, of course, that it should be sent to a committee because, while we support the principle, there are many details connected with the bill with which we are quite dissatisfied. We are convinced many improvements can be made in it, but it is in the committee on labour relations that these improvements will be suggested.
For many years the major labour congresses in this country have worked long and hard to try to secure legislation such as this. Along with those labour congresses have been individuals. As the minister has

said, credit should be given to persons such as the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) for what they have done to bring this condition about.
But we ought to remember-and the hon. member for Hamilton West has pointed it out-that with the passing of this legislation a new day is not going to dawn overnight. This is but a start. Prejudices are not lost with such speed. Indeed I would say it is much easier to smash an atom than to break a prejudice.
The bill is an attempt by means of conciliation to prevent discrimination in employment. That, I believe, is a proper procedure- although behind that conciliation there must be the force of law and of compulsion. American experience has shown us that in the last resort these measures must be compulsory if they are going to be successful. In those areas where there was no compulsion there was a quite noticeable lack in the efficiency of the legislation as compared with states, such as the state of New York and other states, where the element of compulsion existed.
One of the reasons we dislike some of the sections in the bill is that they are altogether too permissive. In other words, they are not sufficiently mandatory. We would not like to see the bill pass only to see it by-passed at a later time. There was a suggestion by the minister which led us to feel that perhaps not as much was going to be done about this legislation as those of us in the C.C.F. would like to have done. Where discrimination is found, discretionary powers are given where we believe the powers should be mandatory and insisted upon. In our opinion the bill would be strengthened if these discretionary powers were removed. In other words, the legislation must have teeth if it is going to be successful.
Then one further obvious and glaring omission has been brought to the attention of most hon. members, in that there is nothing in the legislation concerning discrimination against a person because of sex. There are still a number of men-fortunately, a decreasing minority-who seem to think that women are not people. They look upon women as chattels, an idea which I trust will rapidly disappear. However, this matter of discrimination because of sex is something which can be discussed more fully in committee.
Another weakness now apparent in the bill is that it has not outlawed those wretched application forms which insist that an applicant for work must state his or her religion, his or her ethnic origin, or the

place where his or her mother and father were born. The bill would have been much stronger had some thought been given to this subject, and I believe the committee should give careful consideration to the outlawing of such stupid questions in applications for employment.
I have never been able to understand why it is better to employ a man because of his religious belief or the colour of his skin rather than because of his innate capacity to do the work. Yet that is what these application forms seem to suggest.
The minister has told us that there will be a director in this new division, and he added that the cost of the division would not be great. I felt somewhat pessimistic when he made that statement, because I think the government could make no greater mistake than to burden with the directorate of this division a man who already is doing something else. Whoever is to be the director will find that he has a full-time job. This is one place where I am sure the members of the various parties in the house would not object to an increase in costs of a department, if we knew that the division was going to function properly.
The minister has said the government worked with other groups throughout the country to try to create a society in which prejudice would have no place. But if we are going to do that properly people will have to be educated; and if we are going to educate them we must be prepared to spend money. I would hope that the director of this division would not be merely an administrative head, but rather one who would conceive it as his duty to act as an educational spearhead in the fight against discrimination all across the country.
While at times we in Canada may think we are free from the more baleful influences we see in other nations, nevertheless we do see examples in this country which would indicate that this kind of education is required. In my journeying around Ontario I have found repeatedly that many who have been settled here for some generations insist upon describing as foreigners those who have been immigrants to this country, but who have now become Canadians. Nothing could be more distasteful or insulting to a Canadian who has taken out Canadian citizenship than still to be referred to as a foreigner.
It is that sort of attitude which we hope education will change, and change for the better. If we insist upon describing these Canadians as foreigners, perhaps it is because they have lived on the other side of the tracks. In Winnipeg I live on the other side of the tracks. I am very happy about it and
Fair Employment Practices proud of it, because I could not hope to live among better people.
However, discrimination does exist in part of almost every community in this country and, indeed, most other countries. There are various bases for discrimination, but, after examining into the subject, I would conclude that, apart from ignorance and prejudice, the greatest is an economic one.
I recall vividly that before the depression people would live as neighbours. They might be of different ethnic groups but, in normal, good times, they would get along very well and continue to be good neighbours. But when times got hard, when there was a struggle for work, a struggle for jobs, a struggle for existence, one would become afraid of the other. He would have the fear that the other might take his job, his very means of existence. When such conditions occur, instead of being good neighbours these people become hostile to each other, if not indeed enemies.
One of the best ways to avoid discrimination is to create and to maintain a society in which there is full employment. In my experience the chief forms of discrimination have been by and large against working people. Anyone who has studied the history of our labour organizations knows full well that race hatred has been used on many occasions as a weapon with which to destroy organized labour. I suppose that that is why labour is such a strong advocate of legislation such as this.
The union to which I belong, the united packinghouse workers, has as its symbol two clasped hands, one black and the other white. The two colours together indicate not only neighbourliness but brotherhood. It is quite understandable why a trade union should have such a symbol. I think labour realizes better than most that racial intolerance, racial prejudice and racial hatred is one of the most dangerous fifth columns we can have in this country and of course it shows itself in practice by discrimination against individuals.
Some years ago I introduced legislation before the house which was not dissimilar to what the minister hopes to achieve in this bill. That legislation did not get very far. Obviously this will get much further. I have been so much impressed with what I have seen of the effects of discrimination that I do not think it can be handled adequately except by an amendment to the Criminal Code. In its effect upon people racial discrimination is vicious and should be made a criminal offence. Discrimination against an individual is an insult to that man or woman, an insult to the inherent dignity of the individual, and it should be punished accordingly.
3768	HOUSE OF
Fair Employment Practices
Our experience has been that discrimination has been practised against many of the minorities in this country. We seem to forget that this is a nation of minorities, that there is no one in the majority. When anyone is hurt we should be ready to go to his rescue immediately lest we ourselves suffer in the long run.
I know of many cases where Canadians of Ukrainian descent have complained of discrimination and on examination it has been proved to be well founded. Yet Canadians of Ukrainian descent have been among the hardest workers in this country. They were settled on sparse land and they made gardens out of what was almost desert. They worked day and night to earn a living for themselves and to educate their children. The sons of those people have risen to high positions in many walks of Canadian life. They are to be found at the bar, in commerce and, as this house knows, in politics. As one who lived among them I can say that the record of their sons, and indeed their daughters, during the last war was second to none as the honour rolls of Winnipeg schools can well testify.
They take their citizenship most seriously.
I remember when there was a provincial election in Manitoba two or three years ago a Canadian of Ukrainian descent who was 72 years of age decided it was his duty as a Canadian citizen to get out and vote although he was sick in bed. He attempted to get to the voting booth but before he could enter it he dropped dead. That man took his citizenship most seriously indeed. It is intolerable that Canadians such as these should be discriminated against as they have been in the past.
One of the reasons why we support this legislation is our hope and belief that it may help groups such as this. There are others with whom I am well acquainted who have suffered just as badly, and I speak now of citizens of the Jewish faith. Anti-semitism I am afraid is something which is always latent, not the least among employers. In my professional experience I have come across employers who refuse under any circumstances and for no good reason to employ one of the Jewish faith. No reason can be given except that of ignorance. Such ignorance can be dispelled only by educational processes carried out, I would hope, by the minister's department and other institutions and organizations in this country.
I have found discrimination against the Jewish people in every walk of life in Canada, from the universities down through every occupation. Yet who is there to deny that the Jews have made a most distinguished contribution to Canadian life and culture? We can only hope that this legislation will do


something to help those who have been so often and so unjustly discriminated against and against whom the hands of their fellow-men have been so often raised.
There are other groups which will hope for relief and help from legislation such as this. A young Polish-Canadian of Winnipeg gave his life during the last war. He was a pilot of a bomber and he ordered his crew to bail out while he continued to fly the bomber until it disintegrated in the air. He was given the Victoria Cross posthumously for his heroism. Yet his people have suffered. Canadians of Polish descent have been among our hardest workers and have contributed much to Canadian life. It is wrong that people such as these who are Canadian citizens should be discriminated against because of their religious views or because they bear names which do not seem to suit Anglo-Saxon employers.
I have brought to the attention of the House of Commons previously the case of certain Canadians of German origin whose sons and daughters were in the armed forces but who were compelled to report month after month to the mounted police who thought perhaps they might be disloyal. This sort of discrimination unhappily runs through almost every segment of our society.
Not the least of those affected are our coloured people. There are not many of them, yet they have suffered as have many other groups, although they are good, law-abiding citizens. Two days ago I happened to be passing through Dresden, and I could not help but think of the wretched action which had brought such notoriety to that community. I have heard of many examples of discrimination against people because they were coloured.
Marisse Scott of Owen Sound hoped to work in a hospital in that town but she was refused employment because the colour of her skin was not acceptable to the hospital authorities. They said to her, "we are sorry, but we do not accept coloured girls." She could not get employment in the vocation which she had decided she wanted to follow, that of nursing. But her parents were not content to let it go at that and they took the matter up further. The trades union congresses of Canada took up the matter and finally Father O'Reilly of Guelph, Ontario, persuaded St. Joseph's hospital to let this young girl work there. She was given employment in that hospital, and all credit to the authorities. She turned out to be a most excellent nurse.
This sort of enormity against human beings has to stop and I can only hope that this legislation will help to stop such stupidity.

I hope that this legislation will really have teeth in it. Yet history of the past has shown that on occasion after occasion employers have opposed such legislation on the ground that they did not really need it and it would interfere with their freedom to hire whom they liked, and all the rest of the usual conventional excuses. But Business Week, a reputable businessmen's magazine, had this to say about the United States experience:
Employers agree that FEPC laws have not caused near the luss that opponents predicted. Disgruntled job seekers have not swarmed commissions with complaints. Personnel friction has not been at all serious.
We will find exactly the same thing in Canada. Then Mr. Arnold Forster in Personnel Journal said:
Some businessmen have worried that FEPC would involve them in endless red tape and in complicated legal proceedings, but again the statistics show that these fears are unfounded and that voluntary adherence to the law has been the rule rather than the exception.
The time is coming, and I hope it comes soon, when we shall all realize that discrimination against human beings is wasteful socially and economically. What is more important, discrimination against human beings is morally indefensible. It has been put no better than by the most Rev. Bernard J. Shiel, auxiliary bishop of Chicago, when he said:
A fair employment practices law would give legal recognition to the God-given dignity which every human being possesses. If we are truly Christian, we cannot preach one thing and practice another . . . Economic discrimination is immoral; it is clearly sinful. How long can we expect to sit by while children of God find their paths blocked at every point by the forces of bigotry and discrimination?
We have sat by for a long time. Now we are taking the first step forward, and it is a step which we in the C.C.F. most warmly welcome.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take very long to discuss this bill on this occasion. I think it is generally conceded in all parts of the house that the general principle of the bill is going to be accepted as a step in the right direction. Therefore we in this party have no hesitancy in accepting the general principle of the bill. When it comes before the committee no doubt there will be some argument with respect to certain sections and some changes will have to be made, but I think we can all agree on the general principle.
It has been pointed out that Canada is a great nation, and we all recognize that fact. One of the obligations which we as Canadians must assume is that of seeing to
Fair Employment Practices it that everybody has the opportunity to be employed. Certainly in our country there should be no lack of opportunity, and when those opportunities present themselves it should be the privilege of any Canadian to make his livelihood by being employed in the development of the resources of the country. In my judgment the bill provides a basis, at least, whereby all can enjoy the opportunities presented by our country.
Generally speaking I think nearly all industries and individuals would like to be as fair as they can to their employees in giving employment regardless of race, religion or colour, but it seems to me that many of the difficulties that present themselves to such employers are not nearly so great as they imagine. I believe that one of the difficulties in enforcing a law such as this is not going to be so much the question of legal enforcement as it is going to be a matter of education. When we get our people educated to the point where race, religion, creed or colour make no difference, I think we will have gone a long way in getting over the racial, religious and colour difficulty.
I do not believe there are very many members of the house who have not had a great number of letters and other communications from women's organizations throughout the country presenting the problem with which they are faced. They contend, and probably rightly so, that one of the faults of the bill lies in the fact that no provision is made against discrimination as to sex. When the bill goes before the committee I think every opportunity should be given to the women's organizations to present their briefs and support their claims. Then the members of the committee will be in a much better position to judge what action should be taken.
There is also another form of discrimination so far as labour is concerned that is not mentioned in the bill and which is becoming very widely practised in this country. I refer to discrimination on the ground of age. It seems to be the current practice of industry now to retire a fellow when he reaches approximately 50 years of age whether or not he has sufficient pension or income to take care of him. When he reaches 60 they are mighty sure that he is old enough to retire, and when he gets to be 65 they kick him out. One of my friends behind me says that he might be ready to go to that other house over here by that time, but that depends.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF RACE, NATIONAL ORIGIN, COLOUR OR RELIGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first say that I appreciate the kindly reference made by the minister to the part I played in the formative stages which led to the introduction of the bill today. The fact of the matter is that the minister's name appears on the bill and the credit is his, but I appreciate that there is enough reflected glory for the rest of us.
It is my view that this bill does credit to this great House of Commons. I am pleased to join with other members in hailing it as the latest step in reducing racial and religious discrimination in this country. I am both pleased and proud to be associated with a government which is making an earnest effort to maintain this and other basic principles of human rights. By passing the bill we indicate that we are realists and we give a lead to the provinces and to industry. It is now written, it is spelled out, endorsed by parliament and supported by the Canadian people.
As other members of the house have already said, intolerance and discrimination are the two sides of the coin of infamy which has been current far too long. It is the duty of all of us, nations no less than individuals, to wipe out this base currency which is a constant threat to our freedom. I am reminded of the words of Mrs. Eleanor Roosevelt, a great woman, spoken several years ago when she told of her embarrassment while she was chairman of the United Nations human rights commission owing to the prevalence of racial intolerance in her country. These are her words:
Racial discrimination is now an international problem. Each account of discrimination, segregation or lynching discredits us abroad. Racial discrimination is the weak spot in our democracy. We must re-examine ourselves and work out a solution as quickly as possible.
It can be added that discrimination is also a source of grave infection within a nation. No country can be healthy or secure so long as that infection goes unchecked. So far as this country is concerned I am very happy to say that the incidence of acts of discrimination has always been low. I believe this is

due partly to the good sense of our people and partly to the fact that almost every one of us in Canada belongs to a minority group in some sense, be it racial, religious or linguistic.
With so many minorities living together we are more concerned with respecting each other's freedom because we know in the long run it safeguards our own freedom. Yet we must be honest enough to admit that prejudice and discrimination are not unknown in Canada. Unfortunately these ugly things do exist, these cancers in the flesh of our freedom; and they call for the application of preventive medicine without delay. Many of the symptoms do not appear dangerous to some people at first glance. A barber refuses to shave someone because of his colour; a deed of land contains a clause that the land may not be sold to people of a certain race; a winter resort cancels a reservation because of the guest's colour or religion.
Some people do not consider these things dangerous, but they are. They are what Mrs. Roosevelt called "the weak spot in our democracy". If we do nothing about them, if we permit them to increase and multiply, then in the long run we shall be without democracy; for if there is no freedom then there can be no democracy. So we have examined ourselves and we have been working out a solution. Ontario and Saskatchewan have already taken steps along similar lines, and I would like this house to particularly consider the situation in Ontario. I indeed am very proud of it.
In 1944 the province of Ontario enacted a law against discriminatory advertising. In 1950 the conveyancing and law of property act was amended to prevent racial restrictive covenants in conveyances of land. In 1951 the province passed a fair employment practices law. I wish to quote Premier Frost, who is a man of stature and who has a place in the hearts of the people of Ontario. He had this to say on the passage of the act:
I think our people in this province do not want to discriminate. They do not like it and do not want it. The position of the government and my personal position is one of strong opposition to racial discrimination of any kind.
The province of Ontario, in passing the fair employment practices act in 1951, took a great step forward. That was the first act of its kind in Canada. Unusual, too, was the inclusion in the act of the following significant preamble:
Whereas it is contrary to public policy in Ontario to discriminate against men and women in respect of their employment because of race, creed, colour, nationality, ancestry or place of origin;
Whereas it is desirable to enact a measure designed to promote observance of this principle;
And whereas to do so is in accord with the universal declaration of human rights as proclaimed by the United Nations;

There we have very positive, welcome and decisive steps in the long fight against discrimination.
This government is not without credit, and I think I should point out the steps which have been taken by the present minister on behalf of the government. In recent months it has removed, in a number of important areas, the legal bases for some of the more blatant forms of discriminatory practices. I want to review a few of them briefly, as I do not think the minister did himself justice in his opening statement. Perhaps he was a little too modest.
In June of 1952 the Unemployment Insurance Act was amended to include the following subsection:
It shall be the duty of the commission to ensure that there shall be no discrimination in referring any worker seeking employment, subject to the needs of the employment, either in favour of, or against any such worker, by reason of his racial origin, colour, religious belief or political affiliation.
Of lesser importance but still involving the important principle of religious liberty was the amendment in July, 1951 of benefit regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act ensuring that a claimant shall not be prejudiced under the act when, because of his religious beliefs, he cannot accept work on Saturday.
Possibly the most significant federal measure was the recent order in council, P.C. 4138, dated September 24, 1952, which establishes a fair employment practice policy regarding government contracts effective from January 1, 1953. The preamble states: -it is considered advisable that a clause prohibiting discrimination by the contractor in the employment of labour in respect of race, national origin, colour or religion should be incorporated in all contracts made by the government of Canada for construction, remodelling, repair or demolition of public buildings or other works, or for the manufacture and supply of equipment, materials and supplies.
Today we are considering a further step in the same direction but, before going on with that, I should like to put on the record something this house has overlooked. On February 3 there was a bill before this house entitled the Royal Style and Titles Act. There were admirable speeches made in the house that day by all members who spoke. I want to refer particularly to part of the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as it appears at page 1567 of Hansard. His words are most expressive; they are beautiful words, and they ring so genuinely:
We all know from our own Canadian experience that unity between us, unity between all the elements of our population, is and must be based upon that recognition by us all that we are all equal to each other and that all have the same
Fair Employment Practices rights to Canadian citizenship, and that Canadian citizenship gives us equality in every respect with all our fellow-citizens, whatever their origin, their traditions and their cultures may be. It is because our forefathers had the wisdom to recognize that it was not going to be necessary in this Canadian nation to pour all the elements into the same mould that we now have a Canadian nation.
We are all proud of being Canadian citizens because we can be so and can exercise all our rights as such without forgetting our racial origins, our ancestral traditions, and without there being any effort by any of our fellow citizens to make us over into any other kind of Canadian than we happen to be because of our racial origins and with our ancestral traditions.
The bill before us at the present time calls for no racial discrimination, particularly with regard to membership in trade unions. The stakes which trade unions have in discrimination being wiped out are certainly as great as those of management. Fortunately Canadian labour unions have directed a strong campaign for the enactment of fair employment practices, and are deserving of much credit for their persistence in this regard. Their resolutions passed at annual conventions, their briefs presented to the government, their constant vigilance in reporting on discriminatory practices, should not go unnoticed at this time when we are considering this legislation. Nor should the efforts of other groups, religious, fraternal, welfare and minority bodies, who have acted on their own or in co-operation with labour organizations to end discrimination in this country.
I need only remind you that Canada has received since the end of world war II new Canadians to the extent of 165,000 who have survived nazi concentration camps. If it were to permit these people alone to become established and employed as citizens equal in status to native-born Canadians, this fair employment practices legislation would be more than warranted. By this legislation we show these people that their suffering, their persecution and discrimination has been fully replaced in Canada by a sense of tolerance and understanding, in employment and in other ways.
I want to take issue with those who say you cannot legislate for tolerance. This type of remark is made too lightly by people who want to dismiss this problem without thinking it through. Has the Criminal Code not acted as a deterrent to lawlessness and crime? I do not believe it is far afield to say that you can legislate for tolerance. I am convinced that most people are not intolerant by nature. They may, and indeed they often do, fall into intolerance through carelessness or lack of consideration, or they are led astray by a bad example. Legislation in this field can have a very direct effect upon

Fair Employment Practices human conduct. First of all it brings to light the fact that society officially disproves of intolerance and discrimination. I do not think we should underestimate the effect of social disapproval on people's minds. Secondly, by positively discouraging acts of discrimination it will reduce the incidence of such acts and so reduce the number of bad examples which others might be tempted to follow.
I am not suggesting that an act of parliament is sufficient to transform an intolerant man into a tolerant man, but it definitely can introduce a climate that will foster the spirit of tolerance and the reduction of discrimination. Law not only expresses custom; it creates it. I am satisfied that the vast majority of our people are not intolerant, but some of them may be potentially so. There is in every society a fringe, the young, the impressionable, those with real or imagined grievances, who can fall prey to intolerance if it is allowed to work on their minds. If we keep them on the right track, if we show them society frowns on discrimination, if we prohibit acts of discrimination by law, then I believe we will have gone a long way toward eliminating the vice itself. The government, by setting an example of tolerance within its own sphere 

that is all that can be expected of it- can accomplish that. It can set a standard of public morality which is bound to have an effect on industry and the private citizen.
I am particularly hopeful as to the future of this legislation in establishing a national standard. In this connection I recall the experience of the wartime labour regulations. As hon. members are aware, that was a revolutionary advance in labour legislation in Canada. Imperfect though it was, it set a national standard for labour regulations which left its mark on every factory and home in Canada. Then when the dominion partially vacated the field of labour regulations at the end of the war, the provinces drew heavily on the national code in framing their own labour laws. Thus the dominion established a standard and a practice which moulded the pattern of labour relations in this country. In the same way, I anticipate with confidence that our good example here will be followed across the nation by the provinces.
Let no one think that legislation such as this is mere whistling in the dark. The experience in Canada, and in various states in the United States, has proven that regulation of employment practices really works. There has generally been an acceptance of these government standards which speaks

well for the future of human relations. Discrimination in employment can be brought under control. But it is not enough merely to enact the law. It must be enforced, and it must be accompanied by continuous public education. I do not propose to devote too much time today to a consideration of the enforcement aspect, other than to say that there are no great obstacles in the way.
This bill does not have as its purpose the abolishment of prejudice; that is to change human nature. It is a law to prevent antisocial manifestation of prejudice. It is possible of enforcement, and it can be determined that men are denied employment because of racial or religious prejudice or for other such reasons. It is a difficult task, but we do it every day before our labour relations boards when men, who have been discharged for union activity, obtain a hearing and are often reinstated. It does need a patient, perceptive approach. I am satisfied that the Department of Labour has sufficient good men in its ranks to do the job conscientiously and well. The important thing is that the law be enforced. It must not be allowed to sit idle on the statute books, and I am sure it will not.
But enforcement alone is not enough. Authorities agree that the elimination of intolerance depends, in the long run, on a process of continuous education. I appreciate that this matter of education is not one that can be provided for in this bill. I am concerned to raise it at this point as an indication of what remains to be done after this bill has been enacted as law. Education is an indispensable part of the act. It can only be administered with great restraint, and with understanding of some prejudices that, unfortunately, have roots in our Canadian life. There must be recognition that persuasion is generally more potent than coercion in leading men to change their long formed habits.
Just as education may be essential to the act, so this act will be considered an indispensable element in directing men to follow fair practices. Law is the most potent educational force that we have. The lack of law in this field of human relations suggests that discriminatory employment practices are acceptable; whereas the passing of this bill would be the sign that discrimination on grounds of race and religion is deplored by the community as a whole.
Intolerance is the product of darkness and ignorance. I believe firmly that it can be brought under control by legislation like this, and experience bears me out. Our schools, our churches, our community organizations are already doing much in this direction, but their work must be increased. Public opinion

must be brought to bear on the problem in order that we may have not only obedience to this new law but also understanding and acceptance of what it means and what we are trying to accomplish.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think the days of discrimination in this country, for the reasons for which this act is passed, are numbered. Mind you, the end of discrimination and prejudice will not come about automatically. It will require hard work and determined effort. But ours is a democratic and resilient society. It has shown fundamental respect for human rights, and it has absorbed change in response to the will of the majority. The sooner we learn to practise what we are brought up to believe, the sooner we will be at peace with ourselves and our neighbours. The late President Roosevelt wrote just before he died:
Today we are faced with the pre-eminent fact that if civilization is to survive we must cultivate the science of human relationships-the ability of all peoples of all kinds to live together and to work together in the same world at peace.
We add a new weapon to our arsenal for strengthening democracy at home. I close by quoting a man of great eminence, James Cardinal McGuigan:
We must endeavour to accord to all men of whatever colour or creed equality in the fundamental rights of the human person, equality in the respect due to man's dignity, equality of rights of employment.

The hon. member for Spadina also happens to be my member of parliament, so of course I take a great deal of interest in everything he does in and out of the house.
Fair Employment Practices
I believe the principle embodied in this bill is a very important one indeed, not only for the application which it will have to the industries to which it will apply, but also for the educational value it will have on all industries throughout this country.
The fact that we in this parliament are in favour of this measure is a clear demonstration that the people of the country are in favour of it because, after all, we are simply their representatives. This legislation should provide a great deal of encouragement to provincial governments right across the country to introduce similar legislation in the near future.
In Ontario we have had a fair employment practices act in operation for the past two years, and it. has proved to be both workable and beneficial. During the first year of its operation only five complaints were lodged with the Ontario department of labour, which is an indication of how well the act has operated in that province.
Many people ask this question:	Can you
eliminate discrimination by legislation? They point out the fact that an employer can give any number of excuses, other than the right one, for his refusal to employ a certain applicant for a job. If the employer persists in refusing to employ people who fall into one or more of the categories specified in this bill, these rejections will form a pattern. This pattern will make it possible to prosecute the employer and get a conviction. From then on it will become increasingly difficult, if not impossible, for that employer to break the law.
As I said earlier, another important reason for passing this bill, and I believe it is the most important reason, is the educational value it will have. If we in this parliament demonstrate our belief in this measure by making it law, I believe the effect this legislation will have on industry throughout the country will be very great indeed. Heads of companies will then have been given a clear lead by the government, arid it will be up to them to impress upon their personnel directors, their superintendents and their foremen the importance of judging an applicant for a job solely on his merit and on no other basis.
I have found from practical experience that those who are responsible for employment within a firm can be educated to observe the principle embodied in this bill; and they have found, often to their very great surprise, that the people against whom they have held a prejudice in the past have turned out to be no different from all other people with whom they live and work. The resulting effect upon their outlook is very refreshing indeed.

speechtext:
I wish to join with those who have welcomed the introduction of this bill. Credit has been given to certain people for their part in leading up to the introduction of the measure. However, I would rather believe that this bill is the result of the maturing of the Canadian people.
If credit is to be handed out I do not believe I should go without a certain amount of credit myself, because I have given many years of my life to the fighting of racial discrimination, in part in this house, when it was a pretty hard thing to fight. The hon. member for Spadina said that great credit was coming to the government for what they had done. I would say there is great discredit also coming to the government for what they did, because do not let us forget that it is only four or five years since people in this country were deprived of their vote simply because of their race and religion.
Many times I have been amazed and dismayed by the depths to which otherwise decent people would stoop to use racial prejudice against a political opponent. I believe that is a thing of the past in Canada; I do really believe it, and I am glad indeed that that is so. In my opinion racial prejudice and intolerance are not things that are a part of the human attitudes and human behaviour. In Vancouver I live near a high school, and I know that even when racial discrimination and racial issues were at their height in that part of the country, I could walk out any day and see youths of various colours, various nationalities and various racial origins walking together. I would see girls who were Chinese, Japanese, Scotch, English, Irish and every other nationality walking arm in arm along the streets, with no thought that one was different from the other.
I discussed this matter at one time with a high school principal. He said, "We have no / difficulty at all with the race question in this7 school. There is no feeling in the matter on the part of the pupils. It is only after they have been in the universities and are approaching graduation, and are beginning to look for jobs, that they notice someone is Jewish, that someone else is Japanese or someone else is of some other nationality." The feeling of prejudice, the intolerance between one racial group and another, is the result of ignorance and a lack of understanding of our common origin, intensified by! economic circumstances.


I believe I should know as much as anyone about racial prejudice, because I suppose no people in the world were more intolerant not only of other races but of different sections of their own race, than that from which I have come. The Macleods hated the Macdonalds, and the Macdonalds hated the Macleods; the Gordons hated the Stewarts and the Stewarts hated the Gordons; the MacFarlanes hated the MacDougalls, and the MacDougalls hated the MacFarlanes-and I imagine the Maclnnises hated all of them. But that is of the past. The clans are all agreed now that all of them are really the salt of the earth; and if what I am saying were not being reported I would like to say that I agree with them.
Then the question of enforcement arises. I am not greatly concerned about that, because I do not think it will be a big problem. This is as much a step in education as a step in statutory law. I believe we can eliminate racial intolerance and racial discrimination when, no matter what the circumstances may be, each one of us will denounce that sort of thing every time it raises its head, no matter when or where. So I am not greatly worried as to any difficulties that may arise in connection with enforcing this legislation. I think it will operate in much the same way as the traffic lights on our streets. People observe them automatically and almost universally. Sometimes a drunken or a reckless driver will drive through a red light; but most people observe them because they know there is something back of them. They know the police and the courts stand back of those red lights. They know, too, that it just is not the thing to do to disregard regulations which are helpful to everyone.
I am convinced that the great majority of the people will react in that way toward this legislation. I shall not detain the house further, but would only repeat that I am pleased indeed the minister is bringing this legislation before us, and I express the hope that/ it will become law before parliament prorogues.

However, I feel that this is one of those occasions when parliament is really dealing with something fundamental. In my view there is nothing more basic than the fact that all human beings are created equal and that our rights should be equal, not on the basis of race, colour, creed or religion but simply on the basis of the fact that we are human beings.
It has taken the human race a long time to approach the realization of that principle, that ideal, but I believe we have made considerable progress toward its realization. I believe that one of the allies in the battle against discrimination, in the battle for equality of opportunity among all peoples, is legislation. I agree with those who have suggested this afternoon that we need education, as well as other forces, but it is also true that something can be done by legislation. Therefore I am glad to see this legislation being brought forward at this time.
I happen to be a member of the committee to which this bill will go and I shall have an opportunity there to express my views on 68108-239J
Fair Employment Practices some of its sections. However, I did want to indicate my wholehearted support of this measure and to associate myself with the remarks of my colleagues the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and also with the support that has been indicated by members of other groups.
I noted in particular the suggestion made by a number of members that legislation of this kind being enacted at the federal level may well play a part in encouraging provinces that have not passed legislation of this nature to put such legislation on their statute books. As a matter of fact I feel that that has happened already in the case of my own province of Manitoba. Unions and other interested groups in Manitoba have been trying for a long time to persuade the government of that province to enact fair employment practices legislation. That government has shown itself interested, but has been reluctant to act.
When we met on November 20, 1952, to hear the speech from the throne that opened this session of parliament it was indicated that there would be fair employment practices legislation at the federal level. Lo and behold! when the Manitoba legislature met a few months later it was announced by the government there that they would follow suit. So I suggest that there is validity in the hope that although this legislation applies only to workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction, it will encourage those responsible for labour matters at the provincial level to follow suit. I hope it will not be long until legislation of this kind, or even better, will be the rule throughout the country.
I am glad the decision has been made to refer this bill to the committee on industrial relations so we can study it carefully, and so interested bodies, particularly the trade unions which have been so keen on this legislation, will have an opportunity to appear before the committee. Indeed that committee will have some interesting sessions when it meets, which I take it will be shortly, because we will have before us not only this bill but also the subject matter of another bill, namely the one in my name which provides for the check-off of trade union dues, in support of which various labour groups will wish to make representations.
With these few words I am happy to indicate my wholehearted endorsation of the principle of the bill now before us.

But unfortunately there are other organizations of good repute which contribute to disaffection between peoples of different religions and beliefs. I think the government should give consideration to rendering assistance to such organizations as exist for the primary purpose of breaking down this prejudice and bigotry.
It is important to a country of minorities such as Canada that there should be a greater degree of national unity established. I am one of those who believe that eventually this must become part of our Criminal Code, and that injury or mischief to public interest shall include the promotion of disaffection or ill will or hostility between peoples of different religions and beliefs.
In the meantime education can be assisted by legislation. Those who are engaged in the educational field and the breaking down of these prejudices find it most difficult when children, for instance, are taught tolerance in the school and then find intolerance in their homes, in business circles, and in other fields as the rule of life in the world in which they have to live. Anything the government can do by way of legislation such as this to give assistance to organizations promoting unity will help to build Canadian unity.
There is one omission with which I am concerned and which has been called already to the minister's attention. That is the omission of the word "sex", and of any reference to the elimination of discrimination in regard to employment because of sex. The minister has told us that the legislation is in line with the United Nations charter and the


universal declaration of human rights. I am sure I do not need to remind the minister that the preamble to the United Nations charter includes among other things a reference to the equal rights of men and women. The universal declaration of human rights says in article II:
Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this declaration, without distinc-. tion of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.
The fact that the bill is going to the industrial relations committee encourages us to believe that possibly the government may be willing to accept a suggestion from the committee that the word "sex" be added to the bill so that it will include discrimination on the basis of sex as well as on the basis of national origin, race or religion. Certainly our C.C.F. representatives on the committee will put forth that plea to the government, and I am confident that others will also do so.
I can only hope the minister will lend an ear to that request, and that such a provision may also be included.

Mr. Speaker, before the minister closes the debate I have a few thoughts on the principle of the bill that have not been expressed by anyone so far, and I should like to give voice to them at this time.
I agree with everything that has been said about the bill being a step in the right direction. The fact that there will be a national basic law on the matter of discrimination will be a deterrent to those who might practice it. A good example of that is the federal statute on civil reinstatement of members of the armed forces, which is enforced by the Department of Labour. We have not had many cases arise but there have been some, and I am reasonably sure that if there was not an act compelling employers to employ returning service personnel we would have had a great deal of difficulty in having many returned servicemen re-employed.
As an example of how that legislation is enforced, I had a case recently-as a matter of fact I have had several since the legislation has been in effect-of a boy from Korea. When he returned and made, application for his old job he was told that there was no employment for him because someone had filled his place. He asked the personnel manager of the company if he knew about the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, and pointed out that he had a right to re-employment under that act. The answer he got was that the government was not going to tell them whom they were going to employ. That young fellow came to see me. I got in touch with the Department of Labour in Ottawa,

and inside of 48 hours there was a man in that area who definitely told the manager of the company that it was the law of the country, and that it was enforceable and would be enforced. The boy was back at his job within 48 hours.
The fact that this legislation will be on the statute books in my opinion will have the same result that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) described. It will be generally observed as our traffic laws are.
I have looked over the organizations to which the bill applies, and I am disappointed to see that so far as the application of the legislation is concerned the words "political discrimination" have been omitted. In the United Nations bill of rights discrimination on political grounds is also included, and as a member of the industrial relations committee which will consider the bill now before us I am going to attempt to have that provision included. I think it is badly needed because, while government members look upon the bill as a desirable thing and many of them have expressed their approval of it, I want to remind them that there is considerable political discrimination in this country on the grounds of patronage.
I do not have to leave my own riding to give instances, and it applies right across the country. Many times government contractors have come there on some large project, and one of the conditions laid down by the contractor has been that the applicant for work get a slip from the chairman of the patronage committee in the area before he will be employed. Therefore I am looking forward with interest to the enforcement of this legislation along that line. The very government that is passing the act condones, unofficially at least, a system of employment by contractors whom they employ that I think could very well be discontinued under the terms of this legislation if the words "political discrimination" were included.
Then there is another omission that was mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), that of the man who is 40 years of age. Employers right across the country have a policy at the present time under which they will not hire anyone in their plants, factories or mines who is over 40 years of age. That is discrimination because of age.

Governments take the same stand. While we are doing a desirable thing in trying to eliminate racial and religious discrimination, let us not forget for a minute that thousands and thousands of Canadians are walking the streets today because of discrimination against them on the ground
Fair Employment Practices of age. The reason for that of course is that companies that have established pension plans are not employing anyone who is not young enough to make a substantial contribution to the pension fund before he reaches retirement age. A citizen of Canada who has reached the age of 40, and who still has about 20 good productive years ahead of him, should not be discriminated against because he happened to become unemployed when he was approximately 40 years of age.
Another instance of discrimination so far as employment is concerned very badly affects ex-servicemen. The minister, who was minister of veterans affairs for some years, realizes that in every part of the country where there is heavy industry young men may come back from service with war wounds and disabilities incurred during service entitling them to a pension at the rate of 5 or 10 per cent, but in the areas in which they live they are 100 per cent disabled as far as employment is concerned. That is because one of the requirements for employment is that the man pass a medical examination, and when the company's doctor finds that he has a 5 or 10 per cent pension then he is not considered fit for employment in heavy industry and he is not employed. I am sure that members of the house representing ridings where there is nothing but heavy industry have many such young fellows come to them trying to find some way of securing employment.
Provision should be made in the bill to cover the three points I have mentioned, political discrimination, discrimination against young men who may have a 5 or 10 per cent disability, and discrimination against men who having reached the age of 40 still have 20 years ahead of them in which they can produce, but are debarred from employment as a result of the general policy adopted by employers.
I wanted to make these points, Mr. Speaker, because I intend to press for their inclusion in this bill when the committee is set up. I see no difficulty in enforcement of these things. I think the bill will work just as the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act works.
Members can help in this matter of education. Members can talk about it, and they can assist in cases where there is discrimination. If employers across the country are not living up to the terms of this bill the best medium of education is the member of parliament in his riding publicizing its provisions and assisting those who may be affected.
It is not easy for people across the country to understand the mechanics of the bill and
3778	HOUSE OF
Fair Employment Practices to know how to go about obtaining redress under it. The member of parliament is the best agency in the matter because he knows the necessary mechanics for getting redress under the terms of the bill. Example is the best method of education. If the employers of this country desire to implement the terms of this bill all they have to do is put it into practice in their industries, plants and mines across the country.
On the other hand, trade unions have been pressing for this for 50 years. I remember it being a subject matter of debate and resolution in local unions at least 30 years ago. The trade unions too can practise the virtues of this legislation by opening their doors and admitting suitable people where they can be found; and I have particular reference to the coloured people in this country who have been discriminated against for a good many years.
If the unions and employers set the example across the country there will be no difficulty in working out the problem. I am not really concerned about the broad problem of racial and religious discrimination, but I am concerned over the discrimination cropping up in connection with our own citizens, people who were born in this country, because of age, war disability, or the other matters that I mentioned.
I shall not take up more time, but I wanted to let the hon. member for Spadina know that as a member of the committee I will seek his assistance in having these points covered in the bill. If we are going to give the provinces and others a guide in this field, then we should make this bill as tight and all-inclusive as possible. I do not think the time is far distant when most of the provinces in Canada will be following the lead of the federal government in this matter.

speechtext:
I would like to make a few remarks on this subject before the minister replies. First I would like to congratulate those responsible for the introduction of this legislation: The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) who has worked for and advocated this for such a long time; the minister, for his fine sentiments expressed when introducing the bill; and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) for the work she has done on this subject.
I think everyone here is in perfect agreement about the 'desirability of this legislation. As some hon. members have pointed out, there has been a gradual recognition over the years of the fundamental human right that all men are born equal in the sight of God; and this bill gives legislative effect to the aims of the second commandment to love your neighbour as yourself for the love of God. We are all children of the same Father and


therefore ought to treat each other as brothers.
It is a long distance from the old days about which I have heard in my own family. When immigrants went to the United States they saw signs on the factories saying "No Irish need apply" or "No Catholics need apply". I think every one of us in our own experiences has come across examples of prejudice either toward ourselves or toward others on account of race, religion or colour. I remember very well an example which occurred over 35 years ago, and I am glad to say that I took the part of a negro who was refused admission to a certain organization with which I was connected and in which all the others were white. I remember that I advocated that he should be allowed to enter.
I would also say that this legislation owes much to the influence of the trade unions and those who have been connected with the co-operative movement. We had today an appeal by the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) on behalf of the co-operative movement addressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I must say, having been connected with the co-operative movement for many years, that I believe one of the chief attractions to the movement for those who have joined has been the principle of universality, that everyone is entitled to join no matter what may be his creed, colour or race. That gives a feeling of brotherhood, and people work together. I believe it is one of the reasons for the success of the cooperative movement during the last hundred years. They have recognized universality as the first of their principles.
I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that consideration should also be given to the inclusion in this legislation of a clause dealing with political discrimination. Although the minister may have used his influence to have inserted in government contracts a clause that no one shall be discriminated against on account of his political affiliations, I feel quite satisfied, from my own experience, that men have been debarred from employment on government jobs or jobs undertaken for the government by contractors, whose reputation is that they are supporters of the government; and such men have not been given employment. I think that in the committee stage consideration should be given to that question.
I should also like to state that I have received, as no doubt other hon. members have received, communications from women's organizations across the country, and especially from my own part of the country, asking for the inclusion in this bill of a clause dealing with discrimination on account of sex. I believe, and I have been informed by those

in authority, that it is not suitable to have such a clause included in a bill of this kind; however, the hon. member for Hamilton West has on the order paper a bill which deals with this problem and which would provide equal pay for equal work regardless of sex.
I have nothing more to say except that I hope the function of this committee will be performed in perfect harmony, and that we shall have brought back to us a bill which is improved in every respect.
