speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (for the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 329, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, with your permission and with the concurrence of my colleague, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), who is unable to be .present today, I should like to make a statement concerning the bill to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act which is before the house.
Hon. members will recall that on November 24 last I announced that the government would introduce legislation to increase the amount of assistance payable to the gold mining industry for 1953 gold production. I explained at that time that rising costs and other factors during the past year had further increased the special difficulties affecting the industry. These developments had placed a number of mines in a position where they might be compelled to close down. The government decided that some upward adjustment in the assistance payable under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was desirable in order to help prevent the further closing of mines and the consequent hardship which this would cause to communities largely or wholly dependent upon them.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been discussed many times in this house and hon. members are generally familiar with the formula by which assistance is calculated. In brief, the amount of assistance a mine receives depends both upon its costs of production and upon the number of ounces of gold it produces. The bill now before the house will broaden the formula for calculating the amount of assistance for the calendar year 1953 by changing the rate of assistance element in the formula. The act in its present form defines the rate of assistance as one-half of the amount by which the cost

Gold Mining
of production per ounce exceeds $22, with a maximum of $11.50. The proposed amendment will change this definition of the rate of assistance to one-half of the amount by which cost of production per ounce exceeds $18, with a maximum of $13 50. In effect, most mines eligible for assistance will receive an additional $2 for each ounce produced to which the rate of assistance applies.
No change will be made in the other component of the formula. The new rate will apply to the number of ounces of gold produced by the mine in 1953 in excess of base year production, or one-half of 1953 production, whichever is the larger. I would remind hon. members that the mines have a choice of 1948, 1949 or 1950 as base year for purposes of this calculation.
In submitting this amendment for the consideration of the house, I express the belief that it will be of material assistance to the industry generally in meeting its special difficulties, and that it will enable the continued operation of many mines in communities which are dependent upon them.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
The
brief statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) deals with the factual situation concerning the formula for assistance. In my opinion, however, the question on this act goes a great deal further than merely the production of gold and the salvation or the continuance of the gold mining industry in Canada. Vitally important as that is, this bill asks for an expenditure of money to assist in the production of gold. It must, therefore, be considered from two points. First and most important, is gold worth producing? Is this expenditure of money as a subsidy to one industry justified? The second question is, will this palliative preserve the Canadian gold industry?
The first question is the governing one, because if gold has no value to the Canadian economy we certainly should not be wasting manpower and material producing gold, nor should we be asking the Canadian taxpayer to spend this money on it. The question of the usefulness of gold depends almost entirely on its monetary purposes. Here the questions are, can gold help make currencies convertible, particularly the so-called soft currencies? Will freely convertible currencies aid world trade; and can Canada, a small country, do anything in a positive way to assist by her fiscal policy? In my opinion, the answer to those questions is yes. It is because of the importance of this problem which can be called world trade that I venture to take the time of this house to discuss the matter in some detail.

As was evident, and as I forecast last year when the present Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was introduced, the cost of this legislation to the Canadian taxpayer is increasing. This bill is immediate and concrete evidence of that fact. The new proposals are a reversion to the old $18 per ounce cost from the present $22 basis, and the maintenance of the present cost bracket at which the assistance is paid by changing the maximum payment per ounce from $11.50 to $13.50. This means an increase in assistance of about $1 an ounce, as the minister said, on the ounces coming under the provisions of the bill. What this will cost is a matter of estimate, and depends upon production and a further rise in the cost of gold mining. I feel, however, that I would not be far wrong in hazarding the guess that it would be in the nature of $14 or $15 million for the current year.

speechtext:
No, that is the total; that is what it would cost this year. I would be surprised if it did not cost a little more than that, with the increased cost of steel and other materials. I must repeat that the gold mining industry has never asked for a bonus, but only that their product be sold freely on the open market. Unfortunately, owing to deterioration in the industry and the continuing rise in the cost of mining, there are few gold mines in Canada today that could continue operation without this subsidy. In other words the great gold industry, which was last year the greatest producer in terms of dollars of all mineral industries, including oil, is now a creature of the federal government and beholden to it for its very existence. I repeat that the gold industry today is the creature of the federal government. This is the inevitable penalty-it is true of any industry in the world-when an industry abandons the open market economy and accepts subsidies from the government. If this bill has done nothing else, if that simple point can be got across to Canadian industry and Canadian mining, it may have justified itself. This was pointed out by myself and a few others, notably the Northern Miner, at the time the principle of bonusing the industry was introduced.
Gold, as far as Canada is concerned, has three main uses. The first use is as a metal of development. Today, when our frontiers are just opening up with regard to iron and uranium, we should look back and see how these deposits were found and where the development money in the first place came from. Steep Rock may be a vastly larger iron ore deposit than as yet we have any idea.

It may be so large, in fact, that it will actually exceed the great Mesabi iron range on which was built the United States industrial machine of the last half of the nineteenth century and the first half of the twentieth century. This range-and I shall call Steep Rock a range, for that is what it is-was discovered by the efforts of two men, Joe Errington and Don Hogarth; they with imagination and capital disclosed this vast asset. Their venture capital came largely from a gold mine which is now closed down at Little Long Lac.
The Labrador finds would have been impossible without the capital of men like Jules Timmins, which was in turn based on the Hollinger gold mine. The nickel finds at Lynn Lake were also discovered by men looking for gold. The Eldorado pitchblende uranium deposit was discovered because the gold deposits provided the funds for La Bine to continue his search. The new Frobisher exploration in the Yukon, as well as what appear to be amazing base metal discoveries by Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, Ventures, Consolidated Smelters, Prospectors Airways and others, are in large part the result of men looking for gold which started, incidentally, in the tough, romantic days of the gold rush of 1898.
Shades of Robert W. Service and Dangerous Dan McGrew! Today there are, as far as I know, no active, straight gold explorations going on in Canada. Gold prospecting is a thing of the past. There is no surer way to close down the frontier than to destroy men's incentive to look for gold. This is the first penalty Canada suffers because of the belief that governments can manage currencies.
So much for the first value of gold to Canada; and I wish to give fair warning that if the Canadian frontier is to be pushed farther north, if we want new Steep Rocks, new Lynn Lakes, new Eldorados, new Labradors, we must have a prosperous gold industry to help us find them.
I come now to the second value of gold to Canada, and that is as a curb against internal inflation. No matter what the short-term situation may be, there is no real evidence that we have checked inflation. In fact there is concrete evidence to the contrary. The recent settlement of the railway dispute will unquestionably mean greater costs of transportation, and costs of transportation are written into every single thing that is bought or sold. If transportation becomes more expensive, the goods which are carried must also become more expensive. The recent 7 per cent increase in freight rates is, in my opinion, merely the start. The security of 68108-240

the people can never be guaranteed by government promises. It can never be guaranteed through pension plans, and it can never be guaranteed through any form of insurance, so long as the national currency has a constantly decreasing purchasing power.
I have pointed out from statistics of the Bank of Canada that the wholesale price index has shown an annual increase of about 5 to 7 per cent for approximately the past quarter of a century, or ever since the Bank of Canada was brought into being. The wholesale price index has risen, with only three exceptions, in every year since the bank was established. These three exceptions were the panic years prior to the outbreak of the last great war, and the readjustment brought about after the outbreak of the Korean war which, in the year 1951, brought about excessive buying and caused what is known as a high erratic in the graph. From the most recent information, the figures for 1953 will equal or even pass that of 1950, putting it somewhere well above the 220 mark. I gather that the February 15 figure for the wholesale price index was 220-9. With this continuous and continuing rise in the cost of wholesale goods, which is a reliable base index, there can be only one result; that is that the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar is continuously falling.
The fact that our budgets are balanced, the fact that our currency sells at a premium over the United States dollar, the fact that we have a favourable balance of payments in world trade, the fact that we have a good pattern of personal savings in the country, do not alter the fact that we also have inflation. With inflation no man is safe, and nothing the average man can do, irrespective of new and greater pension plans and higher and higher wages, of more and more social security, can prevent his eventual pauperization.
With the shorter working week, with the rise in direct and indirect taxation, and with a constantly lengthening life span, it is now impossible for any man who is not wealthy enough to amass common stocks or other equities, commercial properties or a productive agricultural plant, to retire with any degree of security whatsoever; and it certainly makes it almost impossible to provide for his family. This hits directly at the workingman, the man on an hourly wage. Unless we can prevent further destruction of the purchasing power of our currency, we are destroying his security, no matter what glib political promises we make about it and no matter what wages he may now be receiving. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that unless our currency can have a fixed value in gold we shall never be able to assure our retired and pensioned people adequate security.

Gold Mining
I have discussed the question of inflation. There is, however, the other side of the coin, namely deflation, caused by the fantastic panic in men's minds over the possibility of peace. The communist propagandists must be having an absolute festival over the behaviour of the New York stock exchange, which has virtually panicked over the proposals put out by Moscow for peace. If ever the capitalist system handed the communists a heaven-sent piece of propaganda, Wall Street certainly has done it this time. I would like just to make one comment about this, and that is no country in the world will prosper by peace so much as Canada. The idea that it is profitable to tax ourselves at the rate of $2 billion a year to produce equipment and material the sole purpose of which is destruction and which in turn is destroyed itself after a very short life, is one of the strange mental processes of the present generation which historians may argue about for centuries to come.
If, however, we do have deflation leading to a depression and the panic fear drives frightened capital into rabbit holes, then as gold in the final analysis is the only real money, the paper value of currencies, stock prices, bond prices, commodity prices and, in fact, the price of everything else will be driven down by this action to a point where the ratio of gold to paper approximates the empirical equilibrium formula of about one to four. This will mean that security prices will decline about 80 per cent. I leave it to the imagination of members of the house as to what sort of depression that will bring about. Anyone who says today that the $35 price for gold is adequate is merely asking for this calamity to happen.
The third factor is, of course, international trade. Quite recently the president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce stated that in point of view of gross value Canada was the third trading nation of the world. Whether this is correct or not, there can be little doubt that on a per capita basis we are far out in front. Therefore international trade means more to Canada than it does to any other country in the world, and a solution to the currency problem is more vital to us than anyone else. Canada must trade to exist, and any individual or organization who questions this is a voice from the past and a throwback to nineteenth century Whig colonialism.
In this regard I wish to mention specifically the Winnipeg Free Press which, for political reasons, has been trying to accuse the Conservative party of advocating trade restrictions. Let me say to this croaking voice from the past that were it not for high taxation and the cost of transportation many manufactured

goods could be sold in Canada cheaper than in the United States. I have several instances in my own industrial constituency where subsidiaries of United States companies are making goods cheaper than their parent companies in the United States; but because of taxation and distribution costs the final cost is higher.
The question of trade, however, has little to do at the present time with tariffs. The chief stumbling block to world trade is the lack of convertibility of currencies, and that supreme evil, exchange control. I do not wish to be in any way critical of the United Kingdom government, and no doubt they honestly believe they are doing the right thing, but never in history has exchange control brought anything but ruin. Exchange control is a form of price fixing applied to money. The government attempts to fix the rate at which its nationals are allowed to buy its paper currency in terms of other currencies. The result of this is that, if the price fixed is too high, there is a shortage of other currency. It further creates a chronic excess of imports over exports, which has to be prevented by such measures as embargoes, quotas and absolute prohibition of imports. It diverts production into wrong channels by reducing relative incentives to export. It makes it more desirable to export to soft currency countries than to hard currency countries where there is greater competition. It encourages the continuance of internal inflation; it destroys the safety valve readings by which people can measure the extent of inflation and the degree of world confidence in the currency.
To say that there is a dollar shortage in the United Kingdom is to say that the pound has been pegged at too high a price, and to tacitly admit the error of the $2.80 pound. This I hope to show is wrong. The United Kingdom made two previous fantastic errors with regard to currency convertibility, and for the same reason; they tried to convert at too high a price.
In 1926 the gold standard was restored in England at the 1913 level of around 80 shillings an ounce, equivalent to our old $20.67 price. With a greatly inflated currency base, as well as an enormously increased national debt, there simply was not enough gold to go around at the old rate and, consequently, there was a run on the United Kingdom gold holdings, particularly by France. The United Kingdom lost gold so fast that she was driven off the gold standard in 1931 after the publication and the implications of the May report became understood.

In 1947 the United Kingdom again attempted convertibility at the overvalued rate of $4.03 United States to the pound. This was such an obvious mistake that it caused such a rapid loss of gold and dollars that the most drastic reduction in the price of the pound had to be taken in September, 1949, from $4.03 to $2.80. Whether these two moves, the return to the gold standard in 1926, or the $4.03 convertibility of 1947, were brought about by pride or for whatever reason, they were both fantastic mistakes. Consequently there is today in the United Kingdom an enormous public feeling against convertibility because of these two tragic experiences. It seems strange that a country whose whole life and prosperity were built on free trade should twice in less than a quarter of a century stray so far from the basic principle of free trade in connection with the most important article of all in connection with free trade, namely the national currency, the pound sterling.
Trying to make the pound convertible at an artificially arrived at price is just as ridiculous as trying to sell goods at a price away above the world market. The employment of exchange control, quotas, embargoes and all the other devilish devices of scarcity is the inevitable result. If a currency is to be convertible it must be convertible freely, and the price in terms of other currencies must be decided by the action of the market. Surely our own experience in Canada should be an example for all countries still using exchange control. And here may I say that I advocated, and this party advocated, a return to free convertibility of the Canadian dollar long before the government haltingly adopted it.
To peg a currency and employ control to keep it at that point is like using a fever thermometer which is stuck at 99 degrees. I realize, of course, there are extremely difficult situations in the United Kingdom, and that the problem of the sterling balance held in India and Egypt is a severe deterrent. It is, however, because I have faith in the United Kingdom that I am convinced that allowing the pound to find its own level on the world market would bring about not a decrease in its value compared with the United States dollar but an actual increase, and I am further convinced that if exchange control were done away with there would be a flow of capital into England rather than out of it.
Just the other day I talked to a leading British steel industrialist in the company of a United States banker. I asked them both if exchange control were abolished, did

they think United States capital would flow into the denationalized, now privately-owned, steel industry and provide the capital which is apparently lacking within the United Kingdom itself. They both were of the opinion that this would be so and that once capital was allowed to move freely it would find work to do. Idle capital and idle gold benefit no one. Exchange control destroys the usefulness of both.
The sterilized hoards of gold, whether held by governments or by private individuals, do nobody any good; and it is the evil genius of the money managers, particularly in the central banks, which has brought this about. They were ardently encouraged by politicians of all parties who, by managing the currency, could show at least on paper a fictitious condition of prosperity. I ask anyone in this house what sort of prosperity we would be having in Canada if -we had to go back to 1938 prices. It would not be national prosperity, it would be national bankruptcy.
It is in this regard that the sterilization of gold is doing so much harm. The world's currencies must have a common denominator, and that common denominator must be freely available to the holders of the world's currencies. In no other way can true international convertibility be brought about. To bury gold in a national fortress, in a private hoard in Tangier, in a bank in Paris or in an old sock under the bed is to destroy its power to help world trade.
I have great sympathy, however, for the man or woman who wishes to keep a personal holding of gold. The little man with his defenceless family who has been ruined through inflation from time to time has full realization that the only way in which he can protect his capital, amassed over the years by the exercise of thrift, which we are all taught is a sound virtue and the essence of good citizenship, is to change his paper currency into gold. With proper functioning, monetized holdings are not sterilized hoards in the ordinary sense but are rather the base on which sound paper currency is issued.
Many of the present critics of gold and some economists have overdone the danger of individual gold holdings. They go back to the fable of King Midas and forget that savings in the form of currency, insurance policies or bonds are subject to raids by governments through planned inflation.
The prime agency destroying the usefulness of gold and delaying free convertibility of currencies is the international monetary fund. It seems ironic that this body, set up primarily to bring about convertibility, has acted as the greatest deterrent to this and to world

Gold Mining
trade. The pattern of the operations of this organization is so sinister that some consideration of the bona tides of the personnel should be given. First of all, at the beginning of the international monetary fund at Bretton Woods there was a man called Harry Dexter White, who was reported to have changed his name from Weiss, and who at that time was assistant secretary to the United States treasury and a major framer of the international fund set-up. He was a friend of Alger Hiss and was charged with being a communist and slated to appear before the United States Senate committee. Unfortunately, however, he died before he could give any testimony.
The next communist to be associated with the international monetary fund was Frank Coe, who has been secretary for many years and has only recently been discharged. This man refused to answer charges before the United States senatorial committee as to his communist affiliations. Another man in the organization, Edward Posniak, apparently is still working for the fund. He was called by the committee, but as yet has neither refused to testify nor has he been before them.
Here are three men, two of them definitely known communists and the other under suspicion, who were key personnel in the international monetary fund. I do not say that the international monetary fund is a communist-dominated organization, but put yourself in the place of a communist with executive authority in that organization. What would the communists most wish to do? Surely they would have two objectives. The first would be as far as possible to impede world trade, particularly between the sterling and the dollar countries. The second would be to make ineffective a great United States asset, namely the $23 billion of gold held idle in the United States. Surely the fund, since its inception, has been a prime factor in preventing convertibility and has, through its restrictions, made it extremely difficult for non-dollar countries to buy in the United States. While world trade has shown great growth, it must be remembered that this growth is expressed in depreciated dollars and other currencies whose real purchasing power is now about a third or less of what it was prior to the war.
The other action of the international monetary fund, which is obvious, has been to prevent any use being made of $23 billion worth of gold held idle in Fort Knox. The slogan "Trade, not aid" will be nothing but a pious hope unless some method is found by which the present non-free or controlled currencies can be made freely convertible.

I am convinced, therefore, that long ere this Canada should have stood out against these trade-strangling regulations and demanded that the international monetary fund repeal them or else we should have withdrawn from the fund completely. I believe that just as our dollar, when allowed to go free, has maintained itself as the primary currency in the world, so too, had we the courage, could we have established ourselves as international bankers and made either Montreal or Toronto a world clearing house. It is likely that the United Kingdom will restore the free bullion market sometime in the future, and when this happens Canada will have lost a great opportunity, in fact a golden opportunity.
With the passing of every year the amount of monetary gold available decreases and thus makes international trade that much more difficult. It is estimated, even by figures published by the international monetary fund, that gold made available for monetary purposes runs a bad third behind gold for industry and gold for hoarding. Whether or not the figure for gold being absorbed into industry is a true figure, and does not represent at least in part gold going into hoards in the shape of jewelry, particularly in Asia, is an interesting question. However, the main point is that gold is not being used for monetary and trade purposes, which is what concerns us here.
The figures for gold going into national treasuries or to central banks show a rapid decline, both in total as well as in percentage of production. Prior to the war gold production ran at about a billion to a billion and a quarter dollars per annum based on the $35 United States price. It has shown a decline of about 20 to 25 per cent in the last ten years. From 1946 the international monetary fund has published the free world production, together with the amount of gold going to the central banks. The answer to the question of the disposal of monetary gold is obviously that the controls on gold envisaged by the international monetary fund, which developed out of the Bretton Woods agreement, simply broke down. The demand for gold in the face of the world-wide planned or unplanned inflation was so great as to push aside the barriers. Virtually the sole remaining impact of the action of the international monetary fund in holding the price of gold at $35 U.S. per ounce is on the gold producers and the gold producing countries, by which Canada as the second greatest suffered. We are subsidizing the middleman and the brokers, and a great deal of our production does not go to our friends.
I come now to the question of price. Here I wish to take most violent disagreement with those people who say that a government, generally referring to the United States

Gold Mining
government, should raise the price of gold. In my opinion the United States government should do nothing of the sort and in fact cannot do anything more calculated to continue the present difficulties than to unilaterally raise the price of gold. The price of gold can only be determined by the action of the open market. What this will be, no man can say. The important thing, however, is not the price. The important thing is the stability of the price, and that can only be found by the free market. Unless gold can be bought, sold, exported or imported freely and without government restrictions of any kind whatever, it will not fulfil its function as a lubricant of trade or as a standard of value.
To say gold is worth so many dollars or so many pounds an ounce, without allowing the free play of the world market, is being dishonest unless at the same time the country which says that removes all restrictions from gold and allows anyone to obtain gold anywhere at any time and do anything he likes with it. That is a complete restoration of the full fixed gold standard. This, in my opinion, is an impossibility for a considerable period. There is some belief that the United States dollar is a gold currency. This is not so. The United States dollar, because the United States government prohibits its own nationals from owning gold, is not a gold currency and should not be so considered.
Coming now to the question of the United Kingdom, I fully realize that the United Kingdom and all the sterling area are extremely anxious for the United States to raise the price of gold, and it has been suggested that $52.50 an ounce should be the price. If, at the same time, the United States would return to the full true gold standard at this price the move might be logical. I believe that possibly it might be sound. Certainly it would be honest. However, it would be a very brave man or administration who would stake the future stability of the United States dollar on this price for gold. My own view is that it would be foolhardy to do so with a past record of many years of deficit financing on a national basis and a fantastically expanded national debt. This move may be made and I can only say that if it is I hope, although I doubt very much, that it will succeed.
There is a school of thought headed by a group of economists in New York advocating that the United States return to the gold standard at the present price of $35 an ounce. I have only one thing to say with regard to this, and that is that for the past five or six years the United States has been having an annual deficit of many billions of dollars and

it is estimated that the legacy of the Truman administration will mean a deficit of no less than $10 billion this year in United States federal accounts. Unless the Eisenhower administration makes drastic cuts in expenditure, with a deficit of $10 billion, or a sum equal to nearly half the total gold hoard in the United States in one year, and with a series of deficits of very considerable size in the last ten years, how long does anyone think the hoard at Fort Knox would last if it were available at the $35 price? To talk about raising gold to $50 or $52 alone will not assist in the convertibility of currency. It may bring about a temporary stimulus, but we have been too prone to look for temporary stimulants in international trade and to believe that favourable figures for a month or so mean a reversal of the imbalance of world trade or an end to world inflation.
The price at which gold should be sold is the price men will pay for it in the truly free market. Prior to the war gold and platinum had approximately equal values. Platinum, which has remained free, is selling at about $100 an ounce. Platinum of course is a war metal with strategic value, and is therefore in demand not only as a precious metal but as a war metal, and possibly is an unreliable index with regard to gold. The purchasing power of the dollar, however, is considerably less than 50 per cent of the 1935-39 value. The price at which gold will be stabilized will probably have some bearing on this, and it may be that something in the nature of $70 to $100 an ounce will be the price at which it will finally be stabilized.
As I have said, the price is actually unimportant except to our Canadian gold mines. The important thing is that gold's usefulness as a trading medium shall be restored. Any attempt to peg it at any price, without a full restoration of the gold standard at the same time is useless. Much as I believe that the return to the gold standard is necessary and desirable, it cannot take place unless it is brought about by the play of the free market.
While I have dealt in some detail with the use of gold-and let me say that if gold has no use we certainly should not be considering this measure-I have consequently discussed the international aspect of the subject. There are now two specific recommendations I would like to make to the government. They are: (1) The government should permit the sale of fine gold in bar or other form under these provisions. Without any other change this would automatically mean an increase in the price to the gold producers on the sale of this gold of from 30 to 50 cents per ounce, an important addition under present circumstances. (2) The government should announce its willingness to permit foreign purchasers

of gold to store their gold for safekeeping in our banks, and should give assurance that if, as and when export of such gold is desired by the purchasers, exports permits will not be withheld. This would have the effect of opening up a restricted gold market in Canada immediately and would, I feel sure, have the effect of increasing the price at once to our struggling gold industry.

I am enunciating policy. I wish to bring certain evidence to support my plea for a free gold market and its usefulness with regard to solving the problem of currency convertibility. My first witness is the monthly letter of the National City Bank of New York for January this year. I quote:
On the continent, there is a growing feeling that the ultimate objective of convertibility must be achieved in terms of gold. To restore faith in paper money a number of governments on the continent have tightened up their spendings and money markets, raising interest rates and also the respect for money. Free gold markets have been permitted to develop in Paris and other centres. Government participation to stabilize free market prices of gold could be one path toward a de facto gold standard.
In the past people have enjoyed the fullest degree of freedom and convenience in international intercourse when principal nations were on a full-fledged gold standard. Often when people talk about reintroducing gold into circulation they think of hoarding by individuals. Actually, in a nation that follows sound financial policies, hoarding is practised only by the most cautious individuals, willing to forsake interest rate return for an absolute degree of security. In such a nation the availability of gold for circulation is primarily of importance to foreign trade, travel and investment.
Gold, Mining
This traditional use of gold was presumably in mind when the Republican party platform set out the aim of "a dollar on a fully convertible gold basis."
My second witness in favour of a free gold market is Professor Willard L. Thorpe, assistant secretary of state for economic affairs in the Eisenhower administration. In his article in Foreign Affairs of April, 1953, at page 414, he said:
At least in theory the gold provided an automatic mechanism to correct disequilibrium through movement of gold from one country to another and consequent changes in relative price levels. Today price levels are the result of national fiscal policies rather than automatic adjustments. Somehow a force must be put to work which will bring about the results achieved by the gold standard. In other words convertibility in today's world will require international monetary management of some sort or other with national co-operation. It is a goal well worth striving for.
Later in discussing the international monetary fund, he said:
Primary responsibility for matters in the monetary field lies in the international monetary fund, which is seriously handicapped by charter provisions limiting its operations. Since the international trade organization was stillborn, responsibility in the trade field has fallen to GATT. The United States membership rests on GATT's activity in the field of trade agreements and it has never received congressional approval.
I think the strange attitude of the United States with regard to the dairy industry, under the general agreement on tariffs and trade, is an indication of what we may expect on this matter. In 1950 the United States had a favourable trade balance of $5-2 billion and in 1951 a favourable trade balance of $5 billion.	In the same years they gave away
$4 [DOT] 7 billion and $5 billion respectively. Apparently it is the policy of the United States to have an enormous surplus of trade and to act as a creditor nation by giving away money, goods and material to balance it. That, apparently, is their policy; and what the American taxpayer may think of it, I do not know.
In conclusion I would like to quote as my third witness the report of the Bank of Canada concerning currency controls, and may I say in this regard that I commend this report to hon. members for its clarity and its forthright statements, two of which I shall give. The first is:
More than seven years have now passed since the end of the war and it must be acknowledged that the world is still far from the goals of currency convertibility and non-discrimination:	indeed,
restrictions on trade and payments are in many cases more rather than less severe than they were some years ago.
The second quotation is:
Major reliance in dealing with these difficulties has been placed on trade and currency controls

Gold Mining
which have, however, merely been able to suppress for a period the symptoms without eliminating the underlying causes of the exchange difficulties. Indeed, there seems little doubt that over a period of time the effect of these restrictions is to aggravate the exchange problem, since they encourage the uneconomic use of resources by providing shelter for inefficient production in protected markets and by rendering production for "hard currency" markets less profitable.
Nothing I have said in condemnation of currency controls goes farther than this. The question of gold is not an academic one. Its solution is fundamental to international trade, particularly trade between Canada and the sterling countries. It should be emphasized constantly that over half the trade of the world is still being done in sterling. The sterling markets are most important to us for agricultural produce because the sterling area is largely complementary to our agricultural economy, whereas the United States is competitive. Practically nothing is grown in Canada that is not grown in the United States. Depressed Canadian prices generally coincide v/ith depressed United States prices.
If our agricultural produce is to find steady, continuous and adequate markets, a large part of them must be sold outside the North American continent. To do this we must And some way to enable non-North American countries to provide the machinery whereby convertibility of all currencies is free and open and not at the behest of any government. The solution, therefore, of this problem of gold and convertibility is more important than any other to the Canadian farmer. If our economy is going to be truly balanced, then we must strive for convertibility so we can sell freely in the sterling area and throughout the world.
My plea is that gold, because of its universal acceptance, has an essential part to play in making currencies convertible. My plea for a free market is because it would start setting up the machinery-I do not say that it is the whole answer-whereby we in Canada could provide the necessary means for true convertibility of currencies, and upon that depends our whole intercontinental trade.

Mr. Speaker, those who are interested in gold mining, and more particularly those who are dependent upon the industry for their livelihood, welcome the amendment outlined in this bill. Since its promulgation in 1948 the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been amended from time to time, and it has proven to be of great help not only to the industry but also to the miners, the farmers and all those who have invested their savings in the gold mining communities and surrounding districts.

At no session of this parliament have I missed an opportunity of telling the house of the difficulties the gold mines have encountered. I have done everything I could to co-operate with the government and other members who have the betterment of the industry and the welfare of the gold mining communities and their inhabitants at heart. Every time I rose to say something on this subject, I did so for the sake of an industry which has played a great part in the opening up of northern Canada and the building of our national economy. I did it for the sake of those who have taken the risk of investing the necessary capital, whether in large or small amounts, for the development and bringing into production of new gold mines. I did my share of pleading for higher prices for gold, more particularly for the sake of the
22.000	Canadian miners, the breadwinners of
130.000	people living in some 30 mining communities across Canada.
I worked hard in this respect for the sake also of the small property owners who have invested more than $125 million in these communities. In my constituency of Villeneuve more than 50,000 people are directly dependent upon the mining industry, and another 25,000 are living on farms which would not be worth cultivating if it were not for the ready market which is being provided by this same industry. I am satisfied that in pleading the case of the gold mines I am working in the best interests of each and every person in the constituency of Villeneuve, whether he is a miner, a farmer, a storekeeper or a small property owner. In doing so, Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that I am doing my duty, and you can rest assured that I intend to continue to do it.
While there have been many cross currents in the mining business lately, such as lower prices for gold, sharply lower prices for base metals, and so on, Canadian mining is already a great industry and its future is even more impressive. The progress realized in Canada during the past 10 years was dependent upon the development of the natural resources of the country, and mining has been spearheading much of the expansion that took place during that period. The discovery in Canada in recent years of some of the richest and largest mineral deposits so far found on this continent has given rise to a marked realignment of ideas as to Canada's mineral future. The present pace of mining operations throughout the country strongly supports the new conceptions that have been gained.
During the past six years, however, to our great disappointment, we have had to face the fact that the swing of the pendulum has been away from gold mining. The industry, though still the chief single contributor to

Canada's mineral output, has been adversely affected since the war by rising costs and the fixed price for gold. In recognition of this, and in order to help the gold mining communities, in 1948 the government introduced the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. Before the expiration of its original three-year term, the act was extended to 1951, and at the end of that year the present government announced its further extension for the years 1952 and 1953.
Without going into an elaborate analysis of the effects of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, there can be no question but that it has enabled the majority of the gold operations to continue in production. This act really rescued the declining gold mining industry, and many producers owe their continued operation to this assistance. The Canadian mining communities have greatly benefited also from this measure.
However, a new development in the Canadian economy has impaired the usefulness of this measure. The appreciation of our dollar caused a sharp decline in the mint price for gold, so much so that during 1952 the gold mining industry has been reduced to a condition of acute crisis.
If any proof is needed of the current precarious position of the industry, the reading of last year's annual reports of the Canadian gold mining companies provides it. These reports reflect the seriousness of the situation: difficulties of meeting wage demands, higher prices for almost everything the individual gold mine has to buy, and the discouragingly low price for the final product. This last item is the direct result of the appreciation of the Canadian dollar in terms of United States funds.
In order to realize the damaging effect of this on the gold mines, one has only to compare the mint price of $38.05 in 1950 and $36.86 in 1951 to the very low price of $34.28 in 1952. At the last annual meeting of Hollinger Consolidated the president of the company had this to say:
The serious drop in the face of rising costs of labour and supplies, will inevitably result in forcing closure of many of the gold mines, curtailment of development in others, as well as lessening of ore reserves. Another effect-and probably of equal consequence-will be the end of prospecting for the yellow metal.
The content of other reports discloses the same situation and gives the same warning. The year 1952 was definitely a rugged year for gold mining. Some mines have been forced to close down and others were being placed in a position where they might have to take the same step were it not for the amendments contained in this bill, and which were outlined in a statement made in the
Gold Mining
house last November by the Minister of Finance.
The government's interest in gold mining is evidenced by the assistance it provides, and the facts show that it has done and is doing a real job in keeping alive a considerable number of mines which otherwise would have had to close their doors. The sympathetic consideration received from this government is gratefully acknowledged by the producers, by the miners, by the mining communities and by all those who have some kind of interest in gold mining.
I wish to say again that the producers have always been aware of the willingness of the government to co-operate, and to this end they themselves have done everything possible to increase the efficiency of their operations in order to keep down costs. Extraordinary efforts have been made to stem the rising tide. Expansion of mill capacity, aggressive exploration programs and a high degree of mechanization have only partly offset the tightening squeeze. Every practicable method has been adopted to improve efficiency.
The miners are also doing their share in trying to help the situation. They understand that the gold mines are not in a position to increase wages and they are willing to co-operate by being patient and hoping that better days are not too far ahead. A large number of them remember the time of the depression in 1931 when the gold mines did not take advantage of the situation, but instead kept on paying the highest wage rates in the country. Our miners are working hard in order to produce more. In co-operation with management they are doing everything they can in order to keep costs down as much as possible.
Our gold miners do their jobs with care and ability, they are safety conscious; and on this subject I wish to mention that only two weeks ago the personnel of Canadian Malartic Gold Mines Limited won the John T. Ryan national awards for safety for the second year in succession. Last year's presentation of the trophies to the employees of Canadian Malartic was made by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prud-ham) on the occasion of his visit to the district. In 1950 the trophies were won by Sigma Mines of Val d'Or and in 1948 and 1949 they were awarded to two gold mines in Ontario. Everyone interested in the industry feels a glow of satisfaction that a gold mine has again won nation-wide recognition as the safest metalliferous mine in Canada. This is an outstanding record, and without the co-operation, interest and ability of the miners and surface employees of Canadian Malartic such a record could never have been won.

Gold Mining
Obviously there is a limit to such process of increasing efficiency and improving methods of working. The time will come when there will have to be another readjustment of wage rates, and in view of this I want to. point out again the urgent need to stabilize and if at all possible improve the prospects of the gold mining industry.
It is recognized that it is impossible for Canada, as a producer and seller of gold, to dictate a price to the buyers. It is also recognized that an increase in the official price of gold cannot be accomplished without the co-operation of the United States and that may not be easily obtained. However, we feel that if Canada is not to lose its gold mining industry and the communities dependent on it, a revaluation of gold is a vital necessity.
As a result of the present unrealistic price of gold the total world production is not very much more than 60 per cent of what it was before the war; and, moreover, a large percentage of the newly mined gold is passing into the hands of hoarders. Very few people realize that the total production of gold amounts to about only fifty cents per head per year in the west, and it takes very little public buying to eat that up. In a sense, the western people are being returned slowly but surely to the early days when gold was practically unknown, and when the monetary system was primitive.
We are not the only ones concerned with this problem. A rise in the price of gold would be beneficial not only to a few but to all the western world. The world productive invested capital has more than doubled during the past two decades. The economic production in many war-torn nations has, in monetary volume, increased as much as 40 per cent over pre-war. The costs of goods and services have also about doubled. In contrast, the dollar value of government gold has only increased a fraction as compared to the increase in dollar volume of international trade settlements.
With higher prices for commodities and an ever-growing volume in world trade, the balance of payments between countries has become an acute problem. As a consequence of this, trade has been restricted with some countries and unrealistic barter agreements have been made with others. Obviously an increase in the price of gold is the only solution to obtain proper balance of trade.
Increasingly lower production of the yellow metal and the loss of newly mined gold are serious matters, and they should be remedied. At this point I wish to quote from an article

which appeared in the October 1952 issue of the Pre-Cambrian. It says:
It is felt that the remarkable growth of populations, the tremendous increase of governmental financial responsibilities cannot be reconciled with the loss of new gold.
Military defence of our way of life requires strong moneys, hence an ample supply of gold.
There is little hope of bringing about a dishoarding of gold at the present price levels. The unproductive French attempt, by way of a gold-plated loan was dramatic evidence of this-it brought in one per cent of French private hoards.
To activate gold production, to encourage dishoarding, to lessen private buying, and thus bring gold into the hands and uses of the governments there is one procedure open. It is the simple one of raising the official price, uniformly.
Leading economists feel that a higher statutory price will not induce inflation. It will recognize the inflation which we already have. It will bring uniformity to the economies of the western world.
There is another school of thought concerning the revaluation of gold, and that is raising the price of only the newly mined gold. However impractical this may seem to be, I wish to quote from an article by Patrick Maitland writing from London in the Toronto Telegram. In part Mr. Maitland said this:
One difficulty facing the British negotiators is the strongly deflationist attitude of Mr. Humphrey, the new secretary of the treasury. He is anxious not to be caught giving anything away, and his entire outlook is hostile to one particular remedy for the dollar crisis agreed upon at the commonwealth economic conference last November. The remedy is to raise the price of gold.
A report published in New York last summer by a group of former Marshall aid officials in London insisted that the price of gold was a cardinal feature of the whole problem.
They pointed out that before the war the sterling area only balanced its trade with the dollar area thanks to sales of newly mined gold at the rate of $500 million a year.
These sales, concealing the true trading position, meant that even then there was a dollar problem. For newly mined gold apart, the sterling area would have been in deficit with the dollar area, despite the flow of income from foreign investments.
However, it was a significant enough feature of the relations between the two areas to be singled out by the former Marshall aid mission in London.
The implied conclusion was:	Since the price
of every other commodity on the world market had risen meantime, a comparable rise in the price of newly mined gold would go far to correcting the present state of unbalance.
It is fully appreciated that this question of raising the price of gold is a highly complex problem concerning which the Canadian government is not in a position to take entirely independent action. However, during the last five or six years, on different occasions, Canada has pressed upon the monetary fund the difficulties encountered by the Canadian gold mines. We are also aware that Canada supported a request for a higher

price for gold during the commonwealth conference of last fall. The government is to be congratulated.
Canada and other countries of the commonwealth are the principal gold producers of the world, and they would certainly derive advantages from an increase in the price of gold. For that reason it is to be hoped that this very important question was included in the recent talks in Washington. We are hopeful that an increased price will result from these negotiations. When interest in gold revives, as I am confident it will, Canada will have a much better chance of turning up new base metal mines as well as new gold mines. It was the search for gold that turned up 90 per cent of the base metal mines we now have. This is the kind of history that could repeat itself.

This group supports this measure because it does seriously affect the lives of a large number of Canadians under present conditions and circumstances. As the hon. member who preceded me said, it affects the lives of, I believe, some 130,000, including miners and their dependents. It also affects those who service the various mining communities and those who make a living by supplying agricultural and other products to those communities. We support it because of the large investment in homes in the gold mining communities. We support it because of the large investment in business premises and service facilities. We support it because of the municipal, provincial and federal government expenditures that have been made. On those grounds, and as a temporary palliative to meet a peculiar present situation, this group supports this measure.
I understand that the amount of the subsidy paid out last year in the way of gold mining assistance was something in the neighbourhood of $10 million. On that basis the gold mining industry, in relation to the size of other industries, is the most highly subsidized industry in Canada. I think that is a correct statement.
Before concluding my remarks I should like to point out that here is a well-established

Gold Mining
industry which finds it necessary to come to the government for assistance under these circumstances and conditions. We hear much about free enterprise from hon. members, but in reality it does not exist today when you have an industry like this which cannot survive unless the government provides some assistance. That is why we consider that this is simply another illustration of the fact that those who insist that we live in a free enterprise country are speaking in the terms of midVictorian days.
We of this group want to add briefly to what we have to say in support of this measure at this time that if the government would subsidize agricultural production to the same extent, to the same percentage and degree as it finds it necessary to subsidize the gold mining industry at this time, we would have stability in agriculture. We suggest that if it can be done for the gold mining industry, it can be done for the agricultural industry.
There is a great need for houses in Canada at this time. For years we in this group have urged the government to subsidize low rental housing. We say that if we can subsidize the gold mining industry-and we support the measure-we can subsidize low rental housing and do something about having the homes built that are necessary at this time.
With these brief remarks I once again emphasize the fact that as a particularly necessary palliative of capitalism under present circumstances we endorse and support this measure.

There are just a few words I want to say on this measure. I notice in the report on the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for March, 1952, that the purpose of the act is stated in these words:
It was designed primarily to assist the high-cost or marginal mines to continue in operation over a difficult period and to maintain their dependent communities.
The question one is bound to ask is how many communities are we going to maintain in Canada and at how great a cost are we prepared to maintain them? For how many years are we going to continue to maintain them? I recall that last year when we were discussing the question of selling wheat in the domestic market in Canada at the world market price rather than the international wheat agreement price, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated that he was not prepared to tax the people of Canada for the purpose of subsidizing the wheat grower. Apparently we are quite prepared to subsidize the gold mining industry in order to make it possible for them to meet their costs of production. When it is suggested
[Mr. Herridge.l
that we subsidize certain other industries it is said that we would not be justified in taxing the people of Canada in order to do it.
I was quite interested in an editorial which appeared in a good Conservative paper, the Calgary Herald, dealing with this question of gold. I draw it especially to the attention of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). This was published in the issue of November 8, 1952, and reads:
How Much is Gold Really Worth?
According to Mr. Drew, the Leader of the Opposition in Ottawa, it is an "extraordinary course" for Canadian gold to be sold to the United States at "less than the cost of production". Mr. Drew argues that this is, in effect, a subsidy paid by Canada to the United States government.
It is natural, we suppose, for a politician with an Ontario background to be concerned over the price of gold. Gold mining and the Toronto financial market have always been closely interlinked. It is true, also, that the gold mining industry provides a considerable amount of employment in northern Ontario. But we have never really been able to see why the business of mining gold should get such special treatment from governments which do not seem to care particularly whether the Alberta coal mining industry, say, goes under from lack of markets.
Except in the monetary sense, gold is not a particularly useful commodity. It makes pretty jewellery, tarnish-proof wedding rings (which do not, however, wear very well unless the gold is subjected to considerable adulteration), satisfactory fountain-pen nibs and gilt for the sign on lawyers' office doors. Beyond this, it is hard to think of any purely functional uses for gold. The world, in fact, could probably survive very nicely if all the gold in it disappeared tomorrow morning.
The only factor which makes it worth while mining gold at all is the fact that governments are prepared to accept it as a medium, of exchange. In the most literal sense it is true, today, to say that gold is as good as dollars-at any rate so long as the United States government, with its vaults at Fort Knox already bulging with the stuff, is prepared to go on importing it, in unlimited quantities, at 35 American dollars per fine ounce. But if both the U.S. and British governments announced tomorrow that they were no longer prepared to accept gold at any price, every gold mine in the world would shut down, since the supply of industrial gold is already fully assured for thousands of years.
Gold, in fact, is a colossal (though quite useful) fiction. As a utilitarian metal, its values are restricted. The only reason it is worth even as much as $35 U.S. an ounce is that this is what the U.S. government is prepared to pay. We should probably be grateful to Uncle Sam for offering to pay as much as he does.
I agree wholeheartedly with that argument. That was a good Tory paper, the Calgary Herald.

I would point out that gold
mining is the most highly subsidized industry in Canada today. Last year the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) criticized a member of the C.C.F. for suggesting that the subsidy paid to gold mines was greater than that paid to the wheat growers. He referred to the fact that during the past ten years agriculture had received something in the neighbourhood of $900 million, taking into consideration all payments such as those for drought relief, freight assistance, P.F.R.A., foot-and-mouth disease and various consumer subsidies.
I would point out that the amount paid to the gold mining industry is very much greater than the amount paid to agriculture, because if the subsidies to agriculture were in proportion to those paid to the gold mining industry, on the basis of population, in those ten years agriculture would have received $4,000 million instead of $900 million. I say that because on April 6, 1951, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) is reported on page 1705 of Hansard, as having said:
The gold mines now in operation give employment to about 23,000 people.
Mind you, only about 23,000 people. Farm workers, on the other hand, according to the statistical review for March, 1951, totalled around one million. In other words, gold mine workers are less than one-fortieth of the total number of workers in agriculture. Therefore on the basis of $40 million for an industry employing 23,000 workers over a period of four years, the farming industry with a million workers should have received over $4 billion over a period of ten years to be on a parity, instead of receiving just $900 million. Again I say, how many communities are you going to subsidize, how far are you prepared to subsidize them and for how long are you prepared to go on doing it?
When I recall the kind of discussions that took place in the house at the time the $65 million for the wheat growers was being voted, especially the comments of one or two of the Conservative members, I am surprised that they should be so enthusiastic about subsidizing the gold mines. On the other hand, we realize that apparently it is government policy to encourage the production of gold in this country. In view of the fact that it is government policy to encourage the production of gold, and at the same time the price of gold having been tied down as a result of the Bretton Woods agreement to which this government subscribed; and in view of the fact that the price of gold has been tied down
Gold Mining
to a level far below the present cost of production, then I say to that extent the gold miners of Canada are entitled to demand a subsidy.
If it is the wish of the government that gold be produced in Canada, and if at the same time the government will not allow the gold mine operators to get a fair price for their product, then I think they are justified in asking for a subsidy. But we suggest that a far better solution to the whole question would be to divorce gold entirely from our monetary system. I know that is the case internally, but it is not true so far as the Bretton Woods agreement is concerned. If you divorce gold entirely from your monetary system, both nationally and internationally, then you can establish a free market for gold and let it sell for whatever it is worth.
Of course if that were the case, if it was divorced entirely from national and international trade, in all probability the price of gold would fall to a very low level and no doubt many gold mines would very shortly close down. But on the other hand let us not forget that today there is a shortage of labour. There is a shortage of mining engineers and skilled workers, and if the gold mines had to close down there would be employment for these workers in other industries. After all, of what use is it to employ thousands of men throughout the world producing something that has little or no value, merely in order to maintain a myth? The idea of gold as a true monetary yardstick is just a myth, and even that Conservative paper, the Calgary Herald, realizes that the true worth of gold is pretty low.
However, in view of the fact that we have tied down the price of gold under the Bretton Woods agreement, and in view of the fact that the government is encouraging the mines to continue in operation, we feel that the gold mine workers are justified in asking for a price that will return the cost of production. Therefore on that basis we will support the measure.

The situation, Mr. Speaker, is simply that a grave crisis does exist in the gold mining industry. The statement made by the Minister of Finance on November 24, 1952, as found at page 16 of Hansard, recognized the critical condition that exists today because he felt it necessary at that time to announce government policy in advance of the year
1953,	even though the measure of assistance to the industry was not to begin until the calendar year 1953.

As to the bill and the proposal to continue the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, may I say that of course we in this part of the house accept the bill. It is better than nothing. It is absolutely necessary for even the minimum, bare survival of the gold mining industry; but having said that for the measure, that is virtually all that can be said for it. It is simply a survival measure in the light of a serious crisis. Having regard to what has just been said by members who have immediately preceded me, I can share with them the regret that the taxpayers should be called upon to provide a subsidy for this industry; but the fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that unless this subsidy is provided the industry cannot survive. Its plight is just as serious as that today.
The subsidy was not asked for by the gold mining industry. They asked for a solution of their problem, a problem largely created by government action. That is a factor which I think the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) failed to recognize in his statement tonight.

speechtext:
Now, sir, I mentioned that the industry is languishing. Indeed, there are so many mines that are just being kept barely in production today that I am glad the minister has recognized the situation in the change he is proposing in the formula.
We hear members in this house talk so glibly about gold having no value and of the ability of the world to get on as well without gold as with it. I am afraid they have forgotten a lot of history. They have forgotten what gold has meant to this -country as an important element in our international trade. They have forgotten what gold production in this country has meant in former years in meeting deficits that this -country -has had in its commodity trading account. They have forgotten what this gold mining industry has meant in the development of the great northern regions of this country, not only northern Ontario but northern Quebec, northern Manitoba, Yukon and the territories and other areas of the country as well. They have forgotten also what the prosperity of the gold mining industry in the days of the depression meant to the survival of the economy of this -country, when days were very dark indeed. They have forgotten a good many other things which one could mention at a time like this.
Gold Mining
The fact of the matter is that unless a measure of relief is brought to the gold mining industry right now those communities in the northern parts of several provinces in this country simply -cannot survive. Those communities are dependent on the mines and cannot exist without them. Those communities have been experiencing great difficulties for some years -past, as the gold mining industry has struggled with the problem of a price fixed by government action on the one hand and rising -costs on the other. Yes, Mr. Speaker, it would be well to recall the debt that the economy of this country and its development owe to the gold mining industry. We have heard talk tonight about free enterprise. The reason free enterprise cannot operate freely today with respect to the gold mining industry, Mr. Speaker, is that government interference has prevented it. There is no play there for the force of free enterprise principally because it is an industry that is working under the ceiling of a price fixed for its product by government It is not a freely negotiated price in the ordinary sense at all; it is a price fixed by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: And always has been.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Not in the same way as it is now; and the minister is not going to argue that point. What we are working under today with respect to newly mined monetary gold is, in fact, a price fixed by the United States government and concurred in, broadly speaking, by the international monetary fund. That is the situation, and it is the situation that has existed since the war.
Now, sir, we in this part of the house have criticized the Canadian government before for not taking more effective action to meet the essential, deep-seated problem of the gold mining industry. While I have said that this measure is necessary today for the survival of the industry, it cannot be regarded as anything more than an artificial, temporary, stopgap, hand-to-mouth palliative. It is certainly no solution and, as the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) very properly said tonight-and he speaks with knowledge of the problem-there must be a substantial increase in the price of gold if we are going to deliver the gold mining industry of this country from the threat of extinction, and relieve the taxpayer from being called upon to provide aid in stopgap measures of this kind.
Now, Mr. Speaker, since this measure was last under debate in May 1952, three things have happened which have a bearing upon the problem of finding a proper solution for the plight of the gold mining industry. The

Gold Mining
first was the prime ministers' conference which met in London last fall. There it became clearly recognized, if one may follow the press-although the statements which emanated from the conference were very meagre-that on balance the British commonwealth of nations has a very deep-seated interest in a higher price for gold. South Africa in relation to its total economy probably has the biggest interest, and Canada has a very great interest indeed. There became apparent a unity of interest among the nations of the commonwealth with respect to this question, a unity that had not been fully apparent or fully recognized previously.
The second factor, Mr. Speaker, was the change of administration in the United States. Now it is not, I am sure, for any one of us to offer criticism of the policy of the United States. That is a matter for the proper authorities of the United States; nevertheless we are concerned about the effect of that policy on Canadian interests. The Republican party in the election platform which it wrote in July, 1952, included this among its monetary policies:
To restore a domestic economy, and to use our influence tor a world economy, of such stability as will permit the realization of our aim of a dollar on a fully convertible gold basis.
Of course that did not say explicitly that the Republican party was committing itself to a higher price for gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: I'll say it doesn't.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
No, but at any rate it does recognize the importance of gold in establishing stable monetary policies in the world. There can be no answer, it seems to me, to that interpretation of these words:
. . . and to use our influence for a world economy, of such stability as will permit the realization of our aim of a dollar on a fully convertible gold basis.
Whatever hopes may have been conjured up by the statement that the United States government would change the policy that had been previously in effect when Mr. Snyder was secretary of the treasury, certainly there has as yet been no indication that the United States government is prepared to enunciate any policy looking to an increase in the price of gold. But, Mr. Speaker, it is the duty of the Canadian government to put such representations as it can before the government of the United States, and before the international monetary fund, as will represent the total exertion of all the influence the government of Canada does command, with a view to bringing about an increase in the price of gold.
The United States government is holding something like $22 billion of gold of which, we are told, $16 billion are needed for currency backing. There have been rumours

that even in the face of representations from the British government and from the governments of the commonwealth countries, the United States government hesitates to increase the price of gold because they have a haunting fear that such action might somehow help Russia. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is so little that has come on this subject from really authoritative sources that I do not intend to speculate on the subject. I do say that our interest as a country, as a leading gold producer, lies with or in the direction of an increase in the price of gold; and that is also where the interest of the British commonwealth lies.
The third factor of the three I mentioned as having occurred since May last is, of course, the conference Mr. Butler held recently in Washington with Mr. Humphrey, the United States secretary of the treasury. Again there has been little by way of announcement from that conference to indicate what action, if any, may be expected to emanate from Washington with respect to the price of gold as an aid to the furtherance of the "trade, not aid" policy. The Canadian government must have some knowledge of this subject, Mr. Speaker. I think they must have been in consultation in relation to these negotiations at Washington. They must have discussed this matter with Mr. Butler when he was recently in Ottawa. To the extent to which he is free to communicate the information to the house, may I say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that I hope he will make as much information as possible available to the house on this important subject.
On the subject of convertibility, Mr. Speaker, let us recognize that gold has an indispensable part to play in convertibility, and in shaping plans for restoring convertibility of currencies throughout the trading world. There is not very much to warrant our being satisfied or complacent until we shall have brought about at least a substantial measure of convertibility of currencies which does not exist today among the great trading nations of the world.
This is an urgent matter. On September 17, the association of Canadian provincial mines ministers asked the federal government to raise the price of gold. From a Canadian Press dispatch which was issued from their conference in Quebec, we read this:
The association of Canadian provincial mines ministers decided today to ask the federal government to raise the price of gold. The step was in one of three resolutions adopted at closing sessions of the ninth annual convention of the association which asked aid from the federal government to the gold mining industry.
The resolutions were: (1) that the government take every step possible to increase the official price

of gold; (2) fine gold be given freer circulation and wider ownership; (3) government assistance be more regulated than provided under the law of federal emergency assistance to gold mines.
Mr. Speaker, that resolution comes from the provincial ministers of mines. They are speaking from knowledge of the problem with which they have firsthand contact, not only the problem of keeping the gold mining industry alive but also the wellbeing of the communities that are directly dependent upon the gold mining industry for their survival. Gold has lost none of its importance as a medium of international exchange. If it had, as was suggested by one hon. member tonight, why is it that every country in the world, including Russia, is trying to obtain gold? If any country's internal policy might be thought to be designed to eliminate any necessity for gold as a medium of exchange, one would have thought surely it was Russia, and yet Russia is seeking gold. The fact of the matter is that gold is, as it has been for centuries, an indispensable element in international exchange.
This measure is necessary, but it is no solution. It is at best an artificial, temporary, stopgap, hand-to-mouth palliative. What is needed in the national interest is a solution.
