This gave the number of mines receiving assistance during that period and the preceding period, and pointed out that there were 74 auriferous gold mines and 22 placer mines receiving assistance. There were 13 on the free market in 1952. There are only 5 mines selling on the free market now, and 8 have gone back under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act after selling on the free market.
The estimated cost of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in 1952-the accounts are not yet completed-is $10-8 million. For 1953 it is estimated that the new formula for mines which received aid in 1952 will involve an additional $3 million, and for the 8 mines returned to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act after selling on the free market in 1952, an additional $2 million. This will mean a total of an additional $5 million, so my friend the hon. member for York West was about right when he suggested
Gold Mining
this new formula would cost about $14 or $15 million. These figures would indicate that it will be about $15-8 million, or somewhere between $15 and $16 million. The payments will not all be made in 1953 or perhaps even in the fiscal year 1953-54, because of the time lag in assessing claims.
I pointed out that the additional $5 million is not all due to the amendment which the house is now considering. Approximately $2 million is due to the fact that 8 mines have found the free market less profitable than assistance under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. Only 5 mines, as I say, are now selling on the free market compared with 13 in 1952. The total sales are estimated at 500,000 ounces in 1953, compared with 1 million ounces in 1952. The current free market price is $36.75 U.S., or about $36 Canadian, and that has remained substantially the same during the past year.
The following summary of production may be of interest. These are estimates, and they are in thousands of ounces. For 1952 mines under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, 2,970; mines opting for the free market, 1,000; base metal mines production of gold, which is all sold on the free market of course, 530. The estimated total production, 4,500 thousand ounces. We estimate the same production for 1953, but the distribution will be different. It is estimated that 3,470 will be eligible for emergency gold mining assistance; 500 only for mines opting for the free market, and the same 530 for the base metal mines.

speechtext: I thank the minister for the information he has given. Is it any part of the policy of the Canadian government to seek an increase in the price of gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
I have repeatedly stated in this house, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian government, as the second largest gold producer in the world, would be delighted if the price of gold were increased. If my hon. friend is asking, as I think he is, that the United States increase the price of gold, in other words increase the gold content in the United States dollar, then of course what he and others are suggesting is really the devaluation of the United States dollar. The gold content of the United States dolkir is established by an act of congress, just as the gold content of our dollar used to be established by act of parliament. What he is suggesting when he suggests that the price of gold be increased is that the United States congress should increase the gold content of the United States dollar; and that, in effect, is devaluation of the United States dollar.
Obviously, this would be advantageous to Canada, as a large gold producer, just as it

Gold Mining
would be advantageous to South Africa and other gold producing countries. But that is essentially a matter of domestic policy in the United States.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: What would it do to your foreign exchange fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: I do not know. I suppose the book value of our holdings of gold would be increased, and so would the value of the gold reserves of the United Kingdom and of the other countries. The point I want to make is that of course Canada is in favour of an increased price for gold. Why should we not be? But when we are talking about it we are talking about an increase in the gold content of the United States dollar, and we are saying that it would be a good thing for us if the United States would devalue its dollar. That is all we are doing, and if anybody suggests that I should stand up in the house and advocate that I will tell them I am not going to do it.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Will the minister then confine himself to what I think he acknowledged to be his proper function in relation to Canadian policy, and tell us what the Canadian representatives at the international monetary fund have been instructed to do or say on this subject within the last year or two at the meetings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend I hope appreciates that the international monetary fund does not fix the price of gold. The international monetary fund agreement provides that the countries that are members should fix a parity for their currencies, and that it should be in terms either of gold or of the United States dollar. We did have a fixed parity for a time, and we fixed it in terms of the United States dollar, which in fact was fixing it in terms of gold, because the United States dollar is fixed in terms of gold. But for reasons which I explained to the house some time ago we found it necessary to withdraw from a fixed parity for our dollar, and at the present time there is no parity.
The international monetary fund, as I have explained, does not fix the price of gold. As I have said in this house time and time again, in fact the value of gold for monetary purposes is determined by the country which holds the largest quantity of monetary gold, and which fixes its currency in terms of gold. That country is willing to take unlimited quantities of gold at $35 an ounce in exchange for United States goods and services. That is what fixes the monetary price of gold; and this free market has developed just exactly as I expected it would, and just exactly as I have told the house it would. Any substantial quantity of gold which is

thrown on this so-called free market simply has the effect of lowering the price. South Africa deliberately rations the amount of gold that it will sell on this free market at, I think, 40 per cent of its production; and even that quantity of gold being put on the market has had the effect of lowering the price.

speechtext: The minister is aware that South Africa rationed the sale of newly mined gold on the free market even before the action taken by the international monetary fund in September, 1951.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: The international monetary fund did not take any action at all. South Africa did it entirely independently of the international monetary fund. I think we should not confuse this question of the price of gold with the international monetary fund agreement, because they are not really related.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: The hon. member has been lecturing, only he has been doing it on a false premise.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: No, I have not been lecturing the house, and not on a false premise. I wish to put the minister right on that, and I wish to put him right on something he has just said, namely that it was after the action taken in September, 1951, by the international monetary fund that the South African government for the first time proceeded to ration the sale of its gold on the free market. It was selling a rationed proportion of its gold on the free market long before that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: The same proportion.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Regardless of what the monetary fund-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Exactly the same proportion; it is selling 40 per cent.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Yes. Why does the minister say this as though it happened only since October, 1951?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: I did not mention October, 1951.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Why does the minister mention that as the date on which the government of South Africa started rationing gold? They were rationing their sale of gold on the free market before that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
If what I said misled my hon. friend, I had not the slightest intention to do that. South Africa's action had nothing to do with the international monetary fund, because

they started to sell on the so-called free market long before the question was discussed in the fund.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Quite; and we were urging in the house that Canadian mines should be similarly free to sell their gold in the free market and obtain what they could for it. If they could do better that way than selling newly mined gold to the United States government, then they should have the privilege of doing so; and it was only after we lifted up our voices on that subject for a long time that this action was taken finally in October, 1951.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me?

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: What is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: I do not know exactly whether my hon. friend is aware of the chronological sequence there. May I explain?

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: He is not aware of anything.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Yes, without interruptions from the smart aleck member for Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Well, prior to October, 1951 the international monetary fund issued a statement of policy in which it said it felt that it was in the interests of the members of the international monetary fund that gold should not be sold by members into these free markets which were essentially for hoarding purposes. That was not part of the fund agreement; it was a statement of policy issued by the fund, to which Canada subscribed because we believed and we still believe that the real future of gold is as a monetary metal, not as a commodity. We subscribed to that and we respected it.
South Africa, for reasons with which I do not quarrel, decided that it should not adhere to that statement of policy, and it proceeded to sell in the so-called free market, as my hon. friend and I both agree, a substantial portion of its production. Then at the meeting of the international monetary fund in September 1951, I think it was, the Canadian representatives and others pointed out to the fund that if one member of the fund was going to do this selling on the free market, then others should be free to do so, and we took that position quite firmly and clearly. I made it quite clear that we must be free to do the same thing, and we have. My recollection is that the fund issued a statement that this declaration of policy was no longer in effect. That is the history of that.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: There is nothing new in what the minister has just said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
That has nothing to do with the price of gold as such.
Gold Mining

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: We fully approved what was done at that time, the decision that was taken at the international monetary fund on September 28, 1951. It was followed on October 7, 1951 and put into regulations issued by the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: With respect to the sale of gold; let us have this quite clear. There was a position taken by the Canadian representatives at the meeting of the international monetary fund in September, 1951.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: That they all must be treated alike.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Quite right. That is what we had been asking for on this side of the house. We had been pointing out that notwithstanding the policy of the international monetary fund, here was the biggest gold producer selling a large proportion of its production in the free market. Canada, a large gold producer, should not have its hands tied in the way in which they were being tied at that time. We pressed for the kind of action that was taken by the international monetary fund, which the minister has just described, and taken I believe on the initiative of the Canadian representatives.
That was the kind of action we in the opposition had been asking for and pressing for, for a long time. We approved the consequent step taken by the Canadian government in issuing its order in council in October,
1951,	although some of us had reason to criticize, as I said here in the house on May 14,
1952,	some of the conditions attached to the permission given by the Canadian government at that time to Canadian gold producers to sell their gold in the free market. I said then that the terms were too rigid. I still think they are too rigid.
Let it not be said, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that what was done at the meeting of the international monetary fund has no bearing on this question. What happened on that occasion has had a very substantial bearing on this whole question, and I have no doubt that what happens at succeeding meetings of the international monetary fund, whether by way of decision or by way of discussion there and putting forward of points of view, will still exert an important influence on the whole course of events, on the position of gold as a means of furthering international exchange and as a backing for currency, and in relation to the vexed question of the price of gold.
I repeat what I said earlier, that I hope the Canadian government, with due regard for the public interest and with due regard for what the gold mining industry has meant to

Gold Mining
this country, will lose no opportunity to do all it can to secure a better price for the gold produced by Canadian mines.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a question that, 1 think, relates to the clause-and that will be a change. I notice that the proposal is to increase the rate of assistance in two ways. At the moment I am not arguing the merits or demerits of the proposed change, but I would like to know why the minister decides to start the assistance at a lower figure in relation to the cost of production.
He has argued, and the explanatory note says, that the reason for this increased assistance is the increase in the cost of production. Formerly the arrangement was that assistance was given in relation to that portion of the cost of production which was in excess of $20 an ounce. I can understand the minister arguing that there should be further assistance for the upper brackets of increased production costs. But why does he lower the point, from $20 an ounce to $18 an ounce, where he begins to provide this assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
My recollection is-and I am speaking from memory-that when the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was originally introduced the low point was $18 and the high was the actual cost of production. Then when it was renewed for the first time, in the hope that we could taper it off we cut down the rate of assistance by raising the lower limit from $18 to $22.
It is a very complex formula, as my hon. friend appreciates. The rate of assistance is half the difference between $18 and the top production cost. If it costs $60 to produce an ounce of gold, the difference between $60 and $18 would be $42. Half of that would be $21, and it would apply to either half the production or the production in the base year, whichever is greater. Now, there are at least three variable elements in there. I have taken the extreme case.
It is clear that the $21 per ounce would only bring the cost down from $60 to $39, even if it applied to all the gold. But it applies to only part of it. So, as I said in my statement this afternoon, this in fact increases the potential rate of assistance by $2 an ounce. But it does of course benefit more the high-cost producers, because they are the ones at the very top who will get the full benefit. Then it tapers down. At a given point the low-cost producers, those still on the free market, would get no benefit at all from the formula. The maximum benefit is given to the high-cost producers at the very top of the range.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
I have one other question to ask on policy. It relates to the proportion of

gold and U.S. dollars acquired for the exchange fund of this country. I notice on page 25 in the table the minister submitted to the house on February 19 that the proportion of United States dollars has been decreasing, while the proportion of gold holdings has been increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: At December 31, 1950 the amount of gold was $580 million and the amount of U.S. dollars $1,144 million. On December 31, 1951 the amount of gold was $841 million and of U.S. dollars $899 million. On December 31, 1952, the amount of gold was $885 million, and of U.S. dollars it was $961 million. May I ask the minister if this is the result of deliberate government policy to increase the proportion of holdings of gold vis-a-vis United States dollars, and if that policy will be continued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CHANGE IN DEFINITION OF RATE OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Oh, yes, I think it has been. It was felt it might be desirable to increase moderately the proportion of gold as compared with U.S. dollars. It is an exercise of judgment. On the U.S. dollar portion of the reserve we earn something, because those moneys can be lent. They are lent on a shortterm basis on the New York market, and we receive interest on them. But on our gold holdings we earn nothing. So it is obviously desirable to have some earning assets in the fund, and it is a matter of judgment what the proportion should be as between gold and U.S. dollars.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
